label: Hebrews 1:2
text:
The phrase behind "these last days" reads literally "the last of these days" — eschatos, the outermost point, the final edge of a stretch of time already underway. God had been speaking through the prophets across that whole span; now, at its very end, he speaks differently — not "through a prophet" but "in Son." The Greek keeps the article before "prophets," marking them out as a class of individuals, but drops it before "Son," throwing the weight onto quality of nature rather than mere identity: this one speaks not as an instrument pressed into service but as one who by nature belongs to God's own being.

He is appointed "heir of all things" — the dominion Adam forfeited at the fall, regained for the race through the last Adam. And the world itself came into being dia ("through") him, a preposition for mediate agency, naming him active co-agent in creation rather than a passive tool. The word for "worlds," aionas, doesn't mean simply the physical universe — it names the ages, the unfolding stretches of time through which God's purposes work themselves out. The Son isn't only the original craftsman of matter; he steers history's ages toward their goal.
translation: In the last of these days, God spoke to us in one who is, in nature, Son — whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom he also made the ages.

label: Hebrews 1:5
text:
The writer strings together seven Old Testament quotations to prove the Son ranks above the angels, opening with Psalm 2:7, where the Greek word order throws "Son" to the front for emphasis: "Son of mine — you are." Angels do get called "sons of God" in the Old Testament, but only collectively, never as individuals singled out by name; that title elsewhere belongs to Israel as a nation. "Today I have begotten you" isn't a statement about the Son's eternal existence or about his human birth — the verb marks an installation into office, not an entrance into life. It points to the resurrection, where God publicly enacted the Son's royal standing in a formal, official sense.

The second citation, from 2 Samuel 7, promises "I will be to him a Father, and he will be to me a Son" — words never once spoken over an angel. Angels are sons of God only by virtue of having been created; this claim to sonship rests on something no angel can share.
translation: For to which of the angels did he ever say: Son of mine you are — today I have begotten you? And again: I will be to him a Father, and he himself will be to me a Son?

label: Hebrews 1:11
text:
The "they" that will perish is not the earth mentioned just before but the heavens — the Greek pronoun is intensive, "they themselves," singling the heavens out for a fate set against what follows. "You remain" translates diameno, built from meno ("remain") with dia prefixed for intensifying force — not just staying but staying permanently — and it stands in the present tense, describing what is simply, continuously true of God rather than a future promise still to be kept.

"Wax old" is palaioo, "to become worn out," a different idea from the ordinary Greek word for age (archaios, "ancient," old merely by the passage of time). The heavens don't simply get old the way a document ages sitting in an archive — they wear thin the way a garment wears out from use.
translation: They themselves will perish, but as for you, you continually remain. And they will all wear out like a garment.

label: Hebrews 1:12
text:
"Vesture" translates peribolaion, literally "that which is thrown around" — a cloak or wrap, something draped over oneself and eventually discarded, not formal dress. The verb behind the King James's "shalt fold" should actually read "roll up" — an old copying error produced "fold" instead — and the picture is of a worn mantle rolled up and set aside, exactly what happens to clothing no longer wanted.

"Shall not fail" renders a verb, leipo, that means "leave off, cease." The heavens get rolled up and exchanged like worn-out clothes, but God's years simply never cease. The angels belong to that same category of created, changeable things; the Son, unchanging, stands above them all.
translation: And like a mantle you will roll them up; like a garment they will be changed. But as for you, you are the same, and your years will not cease.

label: Hebrews 1:14
text:
The writer closes his angel-argument with a question expecting the answer "yes." "Ministering" translates leitourgika, the same root used earlier of priestly service — angels serve in a quasi-sacred capacity, but as agents carrying out duty, not as principals in their own right. "Sent forth" is a present passive participle built on the same root as apostello, the verb behind "apostle" — angels are continually being dispatched on commission, ongoing service under orders rather than a fixed rank held on their own account.

That commission runs "for the sake of those who are about to inherit salvation" — the inheritance is still ahead, not yet possessed, and angels exist to serve the heirs, not to be heirs themselves. That is their entire job description, set against a Son who rules rather than runs errands.
translation: Are they not all spirits engaged in sacred service, continually being sent out on commission for the sake of those who are about to inherit salvation?

label: Hebrews 2:3
text:
"How" translates pos used rhetorically — "how is it even possible" — a question that expects the answer "there is no way." The pronoun "we" is emphatic in the Greek, throwing weight onto the readers themselves: it is precisely to them that God has spoken in the Son, which makes any negligence on their part all the more inexcusable. "Escape" is ekpheugo, "to flee out from" — the image is of a fugitive slipping free of a trap, and the writer insists there simply is no exit.

The word rendered "which" is qualitative rather than merely relative — not just "a salvation that," but "a salvation of this very character," one whose pedigree runs from the Lord himself (kurios, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the divine name) straight to eyewitnesses. Salvation announced first by the Lord in person, not relayed through an intermediary.
translation: How will we possibly escape if we disregard so great a salvation — a salvation of such a character as to have been spoken at the first by the Lord, and confirmed to us by those who heard him?

label: Hebrews 2:4
text:
The writer piles up four words for the confirming miracles, each carrying its own shade of meaning. Semeion ("signs") points to a miracle's meaning — a mark pointing beyond itself. Teras ("wonders") points to its strangeness — something so unusual it stops people in their tracks. Dunamis ("miracles," literally "power") points to its source — an act carrying God's own inherent power, the root behind our word "dynamite." "Gifts" translates merismos, "distributions" or "impartations," and the grammar makes the Holy Spirit the active giver rather than a passive attribute being handed around.

Four separate angles on the same body of evidence: what it signified, how strange it was, where its power came from, and who was doing the giving.
translation: God also bearing them witness, both with signs and wonders and various works of power, and with distributions from the Holy Spirit according to his own will.

label: Hebrews 2:7
text:
The question "what is man" carries, in its Hebrew background, the force of "how small, how insignificant" rather than "how great." "Son of man" reflects a Hebrew idiom, "son of Adam" — pointing to man's earthy origin, formed out of dust. The Greek word chosen for "man" here is anthropos, the generic term for mankind, not aner, which would mean a male individual specifically — the whole race is in view.

"A little" is better read as "a little while" than "a little degree" — the same word turns up two verses later describing the incarnation itself, so the sense is temporal: humanity, in Adam, was made lower than the angels for a limited time, not lower by some smaller measure. "Crowned" translates stephanoo, the word for the victor's wreath given for achievement and rank, not diadema, the royal crown of an office — Adam's glory was a crown earned by his standing as head of creation, not merely a badge of authority.
translation: You made him, for a little while, lower than the angels; you crowned him, as a victor, with glory and honor.

label: Hebrews 2:8
text:
The psalm's claim is total — "all things" placed under man's feet, with nothing held back. But the writer immediately sets that totality against plain observation: "we do not yet see all things subjected to him." The tension is the point. Adam was given comprehensive dominion, and comprehensive dominion is exactly what present experience shows we no longer have.

The gap between the declared grant and the observed reality is where the fall shows itself: rule lost, not merely rule diminished. That gap is precisely what the verse that follows exists to close.
translation: You put all things in subjection under his feet — for in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.

label: Hebrews 2:12
text:
This is a direct citation from Psalm 22, brought in purely as proof from Scripture for the claim just made — that the Son is not ashamed to call believers his brothers. The word rendered "church" is simply ekklesia, "assembly" — the Son is pictured singing praise in the middle of the gathered community, not standing apart from it.

The quotation does double duty: it supplies scriptural warrant for calling believers "brethren," and it places that praise-song in a corporate, congregational setting rather than a private one.
translation: I will announce your name to my brothers; in the middle of the assembly I will sing your praise.

label: Hebrews 2:13
text:
This second citation comes from Isaiah, where the prophet's own children carried names that functioned as living prophecies — meanings tied to a coming judgment and a returning remnant. The bond Isaiah claims with those children, both of them standing as signs to the nation, becomes the model here for the bond between Christ and believers.

It's a household picture: a father naming his own as evidence of a shared mission, borrowed to show how completely the Son identifies with those he calls his brothers.
translation: And again: I will put my trust in him. And again: Here am I, and the children God has given me.

label: Hebrews 2:14
text:
Two different Greek verbs do careful work here, both usually flattened in English into "share" or "partake." The children "hold in common" (koinoneo) flesh and blood — a nature they possess jointly with one another simply by being born. But Christ "took hold of" (metecho, literally "hold with") that same flesh and blood — a different root, describing something not natural to him but deliberately laid hold of and attached to himself. Humanity was never his by nature; he added it. The Greek order of the nouns, "blood and flesh," reflects a set phrase for human nature as distinct from God's.

"Destroy" translates katargeo, "render inoperative, bring to nothing" — not annihilate. The devil isn't erased; his grip is broken. And "power" is kratos, meaning dominion or sovereign reach rather than mere strength — death's hold over humanity was a kingdom, and that kingdom has been overturned.
translation: Since, then, the children hold in common blood and flesh, he himself likewise took hold of the same, in order that through death he might render inoperative the one holding the dominion of death — that is, the devil.

label: Hebrews 2:15
text:
"Deliver" translates apallasso, a word used in everyday Greek documents of a wife securing release from a marriage contract — a formal, legal setting-free, not a vague rescue. "Subject to bondage" is enochoi, built from echo ("hold") with en ("in") prefixed — literally "held in."

Death, before Christ's victory, held its grip on people across their entire span of life, not as an occasional dread but as a constant, low-grade captivity of fear.
translation: And release those who, through fear of death, were being held in bondage through the whole course of their lives.

label: Hebrews 2:16
text:
"Verily" is dēpou, "as is well known, doubtless" — a throwaway aside assuming common ground with the reader. "Took hold of" renders epilambanetai, a verb pictured from someone grasping a person to pull them back from danger — laying hold for the purpose of rescue. The King James inserts the italicized words "the nature of," which aren't in the Greek at all and actually blur the sense; the verb isn't about assuming a nature but about reaching out to help.

Christ doesn't reach out to rescue angels; he reaches for Abraham's descendants.
translation: For, as is well known, it is not angels he takes hold of to rescue, but he takes hold of Abraham's descendants, to bring them help.

label: Hebrews 2:18
text:
The Greek word order shifts the emphasis from the English: "in that which he suffered, having himself been tempted" — the suffering explains what the temptation actually consisted of. "Tempted" is peirazomai, a word carrying two senses at once: putting something to the test to see what's really in it, and — because so many fail such tests — solicitation toward evil. Both are live here; Christ's sufferings were themselves the proving ground and the point of pressure toward sin.

"Succor" translates boetheo, a compound built from "cry" and "run" — literally, to run at someone's cry for help. It isn't passive sympathy; it's an active response to a call.
translation: For in that which he himself suffered, being put to the test, he is able to run to the cry of those who are being tested, and bring them help.

label: Hebrews 3:1
text:
"Holy" here is positional rather than a report card on behavior — hagios, "set apart," naming a status before God rather than a level of moral achievement. "Partakers" is metochoi, elsewhere translated "associates" — people bound together in a shared calling, here a heavenly one specifically, distinguishing this group from Old Testament saints who could equally be called "holy brethren" but whose calling and destiny were earthly.

"Consider" is katanoeo, "to fix the mind on, examine attentively" — not a glance but a sustained, deliberate look. And "apostle," applied to Christ here, is apostolos, the noun from apostello, the verb used throughout the Greek Old Testament for God dispatching Moses on a commission, and elsewhere for God sending the Son — the same verb, the same kind of formal, credentialed mission, for both men. "Profession" is better rendered "confession" — homologia, literally "speaking the same thing," agreeing with a report already given rather than volunteering fresh testimony.
translation: Therefore, holy brothers, associates in a heavenly calling, fix your minds attentively on the Apostle and High Priest of our confession — Jesus.

label: Hebrews 3:2
text:
"Faithful" is present tense in the Greek, not past — not "was faithful" on some occasion but "is faithful" as a matter of settled, ongoing character. The comparison to Moses draws on God's own testimony in Numbers, where Moses is called faithful "in all my house" — the highest standard of human fidelity these readers knew.

The Son matches that same standard of faithfulness, but, as the argument that follows will show, in an entirely different capacity.
translation: Who is faithful to the one who appointed him — as Moses also was faithful in all his house.

label: Hebrews 3:3
text:
The logic runs on a plain analogy: a builder outranks the house he builds. Since the Son is the one who built the household — Israel, and by extension the household of faith — and Moses is himself only a member of that household, the Son necessarily outranks Moses.

The builder's glory always exceeds the glory of what he made.
translation: For this one has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, by as much as the one who built the house has more honor than the house itself.

label: Hebrews 3:4
text:
The writer heads off a possible misreading. Crediting the Son with building the house doesn't set him up as an independent builder alongside God — every house has a builder, and the one who built everything is God.

The Son's specific role as builder of Israel's house is folded into, not separate from, God's role as builder of all things.
translation: For every house is built by someone, but the one who built all things is God.

label: Hebrews 3:6
text:
The preposition shift here carries the whole point: Moses was faithful en ("in") the house, a servant working within it; the Son is faithful epi ("over") the house, ruling above it as owner's son rather than staff. "If" translates ean, introducing a genuinely open, future condition — not a threat to a settled salvation, but a test that reveals whether the profession was ever real to begin with.

"Hold fast" is katecho, a word used in nautical Greek for a ship holding its course toward land — the picture is of steady, sustained direction, not a single decisive grip. "Confidence" is parrēsia, built from "all" and "speech" — literally unrestrained, all-out speech, the boldness that comes from having nothing to hide and nothing to fear.
translation: But Messiah, as a Son, is faithful over his house — whose house we are, if indeed we go on holding our course with the boldness and exultant confidence of our hope, firm until the end.

label: Hebrews 3:9
text:
The word translated "when" actually means "where" — hou, a place-marker, tying the unbelief to the specific location of the wilderness testing. Two different words for "test" sit behind this verse: peirazo, testing to discover what's really there, whether good or evil, and dokimazo, testing in order to approve someone who passes.

Israel's fathers put God through the first kind — probing him with suspicion, as though he might fail — rather than approaching him with the confidence that assumes he will pass. That's the insult buried in the verse: testing God as though he were the one on trial.
translation: Where your fathers tested me, to see what was in me, and saw my works forty years.

label: Hebrews 3:11
text:
"So" translates hos, "in keeping with which" — tying this verse to the preceding testing as cause to consequence. The oath itself preserves a Hebrew idiom: literally "if they shall enter," a self-imprecating formula meaning something like "may I no longer be God if they enter" — the strongest form a vow could take.

"Rest" is katapausis, built from pauo ("cease, stop") with a prefix adding a sense of permanence — not a pause but a settled, lasting cessation from labor, here specifically Israel's promised tranquility in Canaan, forfeited by that generation's unbelief.
translation: So I swore in my wrath: If they shall enter into my rest —

label: Hebrews 3:13
text:
"Exhort" is parakaleo, built from kaleo ("call") intensified by para — "call urgently," beg, press. The same verb kaleo shows up again in "today," meaning "proclaim aloud" — the phrase pictures someone crying out the word "Today!" for as long as it remains true. The definite article in front of "Today" ties this straight back to the earlier citation, keeping the same specific day in view.

"Deceitfulness" translates apate, naming a trick or stratagem rather than a general quality of being deceptive — sin here isn't described as vaguely misleading but as running an active con. And "the sin" carries the definite article, pointing to one particular sin already named in context: apostasy, not sin in general.
translation: But keep on exhorting one another, daily, as long as it is still called "Today," so that none of you may be hardened by the trickery of sin.

label: Hebrews 3:14
text:
"Partakers" is metochoi again, but the genitive that follows flips the relationship found in verse 6: there, believers are Christ's house, his possession; here, Christ is the believers' shared possession — "partakers of Christ" means co-holders of him. "Are made" translates gegonamen, the perfect tense of ginomai ("become") — grammar that reaches into the past and holds its result open into the present: "we became, and as a result now are."

"Confidence" is hupostasis, literally "that which stands under" — the same word used elsewhere in this letter for a "title deed," borrowed from legal documents that proved ownership of property. Faith functions here as the paperwork underwriting the claim to salvation.
translation: For we have become — and so now are — sharers together in Messiah, if indeed we go on holding the beginning of our confident ground firm until the end.

label: Hebrews 3:16
text:
The Greek here hinges on a single accent mark distinguishing an indefinite pronoun ("some") from an interrogative one ("who?"). Read as a question, the verse becomes a pointed challenge rather than a vague statement: "who, having heard, provoked?" — followed immediately by its own answer.

Not a few stragglers, but the entire generation that left Egypt under Moses. No one gets to imagine the failure belonged to someone else.
translation: For who, having heard, provoked him? Was it not all who came out of Egypt through Moses?

label: Hebrews 3:17
text:
"Carcases" translates a Greek word whose singular form literally means "a limb" — the image underneath is dismemberment, bodies scattered rather than simply "dead." Paul draws on the same picture in writing to Corinth, describing that generation as "strewn down" across the wilderness.

Not a quiet burial, but bodies left where they fell, generation after generation, across forty years.
translation: And with whom was he angry forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell scattered in the wilderness?

label: Hebrews 3:18
text:
The verb for "did not believe" isn't pisteuo, the ordinary New Testament word for "believe" — it's apeitheo, "to refuse to be persuaded, to be non-compliant, disobedient." The word choice matters: this wasn't simple doubt or an honest failure to be convinced.

It names a stubborn, willful refusal to comply, obstinacy dressed up as skepticism.
translation: And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, except to those who refused to be persuaded?

label: Hebrews 3:19
text:
"Unbelief" is apistia, simply "faith" with a negating prefix attached — grammatically the bare opposite of trust. But the sequence in this short passage runs disobedience first, unbelief following as its result.

A reminder that unbelief is rarely a neutral intellectual verdict; it grows out of a will already set against compliance.
translation: So we see that they were not able to enter, because of unbelief.

label: Hebrews 4:1
text:
"Being left" is a present participle — "there being left behind and still remaining" — stressing that the offer of rest hasn't expired; it remains open to this generation of readers. "Come short of" translates a verb that could mean actually falling short, being judged to have fallen short, or merely thinking one has fallen short.

Context favors the last sense: the writer's fear is that his readers will talk themselves into believing it's too late for them, when the promise is, in fact, still on the table.
translation: Let us therefore fear, lest, while a promise of entering into his rest still remains open, any of you should come to think that he has fallen short of it.

label: Hebrews 4:2
text:
The verb behind "not being mixed with faith" is sugkerannumi, "to blend together, commingle" — a chemical picture, of two substances failing to combine into a single compound. The message reached their ears but never fused with faith in their minds, so it stayed inert, undissolved, doing nothing.

"Was preached" reflects a periphrastic perfect construction — grammar built to stress not just that the message was delivered once, but that it was delivered so thoroughly its imprint persists to this day in the hearers' memory. There was no excuse of unclear delivery; the failure was entirely on the side of absorption.
translation: For indeed we have had good news thoroughly announced to us — and it remains with us still — just as they also did; but the message they heard did not profit them, because it was not commingled by faith with those who heard it.

label: Hebrews 4:3
text:
"We... enter" sits in the present tense — entering rest is described as an ongoing mark of believers, not a one-time past event or a future hope only. The rest itself was ready from the very foundation of the world, already prepared in God's completed work of creation.

The unbelieving wilderness generation didn't fail to enter because the rest wasn't ready; it was ready and waiting the whole time.
translation: For we who have believed are entering into that rest, just as he said: As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest — though his works were finished from the foundation of the world.

label: Hebrews 4:4
text: This verse simply supplies the writer's proof text from Genesis, grounding the whole discussion of "rest" in God's own rest on the seventh day of creation — the pattern every later promise of rest, for Israel and for believers, traces back to.
translation: For he has said somewhere concerning the seventh day: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.

label: Hebrews 4:5
text: The writer simply repeats the earlier quotation from Psalm 95, and the repetition itself is the argument — driving home, a second time, that this generation was formally excluded from the rest by God's own oath.
translation: And again in this place: They shall not enter into my rest.

label: Hebrews 4:6
text:
"It remains" is apoleipo, "left over from earlier times" — the offer of rest didn't expire with the wilderness generation; it carried forward, unclaimed. Those who first heard it are described with a passive participle from euaggelizomai — "those who were the subjects of the good-news announcement" — the emphasis falling on their having received it, not on how they responded.

"Unbelief" here is again the "non-persuasible" word, apeitheia, matching the verb used two verses earlier — the same stubborn refusal to be won over, not a passive lack of information.
translation: Since therefore it remains over for some to enter it, and those who first received the good news did not enter because of their refusal to be persuaded —

label: Hebrews 4:7
text:
"He designates" is horizo, "to mark out the boundaries of, to fix precisely" — God pins down a specific day, not a vague future opportunity. The writer flags that this fresh offer came five hundred years after Moses, spoken through David — proof by itself that the rest under Joshua's conquest of Canaan hadn't exhausted the promise, or God wouldn't have needed to reissue it centuries later.

"As it is said" uses a perfect tense — "as it has been said, and stands said still" — the record isn't a fading memory; it's permanently on the books.
translation: He again marks out a certain day, Today, saying through David after so long a time, just as it has been said before and stands said still: Today, if you hear his voice, do not go on hardening your hearts.

label: Hebrews 4:8
text:
The name behind "Joshua" is the identical Greek word rendered "Jesus" everywhere else in the New Testament — Iesous — used of the actual man Joshua in only a couple of spots in the whole New Testament, this being one of them. The wordplay isn't incidental to the writer's argument: the earlier Joshua could only lead Israel into a temporary, physical rest.

If that rest had been final, there would have been no reason for God, five hundred years later, to speak of "another day" still to come. The very fact that a later offer was made proves the first was incomplete.
translation: For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day after that.

label: Hebrews 4:10
text:
The writer returns here to katapausis, the general word for "rest" as cessation, after using a more specific word for Sabbath-keeping just before — a shift from the ideal, Sabbath-patterned rest to the plainer language of ceasing from labor.

"His own" translates idios, a word marking private, personal ownership rather than shared or generic possession — God's works are peculiarly his, and the rest that follows is likewise the believer's own cessation, patterned after God's, not a borrowed or generic stopping-point.
translation: For the one who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God rested from his own.

label: Hebrews 4:11
text:
"Let us labor" is spoudazo, a verb combining urgency of purpose with urgency of effort — not calm diligence but hurried, intent exertion, the sort of word used for someone racing to finish before a deadline.

The warning that follows recycles the wilderness generation's failure as a cautionary "example" — the Greek word names a pattern or mold nobody should let themselves be poured into twice.
translation: Let us therefore make every effort to enter into that rest, so that no one may fall into the same pattern of disobedience.

label: Hebrews 4:12
text:
"Living" translates the present participle of zao — not a past-tense description but an ongoing state: the word is alive right now, actively so, not a static text. "Powerful" is energes, the root behind our word "energy" — active, energizing, doing work rather than merely existing. "Sharper" comes from temno, "to cut" — the comparative form measures the word's edge against the sharpest weapon its readers knew, a two-edged sword.

"Dividing asunder" is easy to misread as one thing separated from another — soul from spirit, joint from marrow. The Greek genitive actually describes a piercing through each one internally; the sword doesn't cut soul away from spirit, it cuts through the soul, and through the spirit, laying bare what's inside each. "Discerner" is kritikos, built on krino ("judge, sift, separate"), the root behind our word "critic" — a capacity to sift and analyze, not merely observe.
translation: For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing through even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and is a sifter and analyzer of the reflections and conceptions of the heart.

label: Hebrews 4:13
text:
"Laid bare" translates trachelizo, a verb built from trachelos, "neck" or "throat" — used of a wrestler seizing an opponent by the throat, or of a sacrificial victim's neck bent back to expose it to the knife. The image is graphic and specific: total, forced exposure, the kind inflicted on something that cannot resist.

"With whom we have to do" carries the word logos in a commercial sense familiar from everyday Greek business language — "to render account," to settle a ledger. Every created thing stands exposed like a sacrifice bared to the blade, and every person owes God a reckoning like an account come due.
translation: And there is no creature hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid bare, throats exposed, to the eyes of him to whom we must render our account.

label: Hebrews 4:15
text:
"Touched with the feeling of" translates sunpatheo — patheo ("suffer," from the same root as pascho) with sun ("with") prefixed — literally, "to suffer along with." This isn't abstract awareness of human weakness; it's experiential, a fellow-feeling built from actually having gone through the same pressure.

"In all points" pushes the comparison as far as it will go — full identification with human temptation, with the one stated exception that in his case it never issued in sin.
translation: For we do not have a high priest unable to feel with us in our weaknesses, but one who has been tempted in every way just as we are — yet without sin.

label: Hebrews 4:16
text:
"Let us come" is proserchomai, the standard verb for a worshiper's approach to the altar under the old system — the writer reuses temple-approach language for approaching Christ directly. Two nouns follow, mercy and grace, and they aren't redundant: mercy answers for sins already committed, while grace supplies what's needed going forward — pardon for the past, provision for what's ahead.

"In time of need" carries the sense of well-timed help, aid that arrives exactly when it's needed rather than early or late.
translation: Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for well-timed help.

label: Hebrews 5:3
text:
"Ought" here is opheilo, marking a moral obligation rooted in the priest's own condition — distinct from the sheer logical necessity expressed by a different verb elsewhere in this letter, and from the language of simple "fittingness" used of Christ's sufferings.

Because the priest himself is bound up in the same moral weakness as those he serves, he's morally obligated to offer sacrifice for himself first — an obligation that exposes exactly what's missing in a priest who has no sin of his own to atone for.
translation: And because of this, he is under obligation — just as he offers for the people, so also for his own sins — to make offering.

label: Hebrews 5:4
text:
The point is procedural and deliberately unglamorous: priestly office is never self-appointed. Aaron didn't nominate himself; the honor came from outside, by call.

Anyone claiming the office on his own authority disqualifies himself by the very act of claiming it.
translation: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when he is called by God, just as Aaron also was.

label: Hebrews 5:5
text:
The writer quotes the same words used earlier to establish Christ's sonship — "you are my Son, today I have begotten you" — reusing them here to ground the priestly call in the sonship itself, not in personal ambition or self-promotion.

The sentence is actually left grammatically unfinished in the Greek, trailing off after the quotation, trusting the reader to supply the obvious conclusion: the one who spoke those words is the one who conferred the honor.
translation: So also the Messiah did not glorify himself to become a high priest, but it was the one who said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you —

label: Hebrews 5:8
text:
The Greek has no article before "Son" here, and the missing article does the same work it did earlier in the letter — it isn't naming an identity so much as a quality: "though he was Son by nature," full deity, not merely one son among others. The point isn't that deity needed disciplining out of some tendency to disobey; obedience, as an experience, was simply unavailable to him before the incarnation — there was no one greater to obey.

Only by taking on a human situation did he come to know obedience firsthand, learned the way anyone learns anything: by living it, specifically by living it under suffering.
translation: Though he was Son by nature, he learned obedience from the things he suffered.

label: Hebrews 5:9
text:
"Made perfect" is teleios, which doesn't describe moral improvement but arrival at an intended goal — reaching the completion for which something was designed. Christ's sufferings brought him to the very consummation his priestly office required.

"Author" translates aitios, "that in which a cause resides" — the point of origin from which something proceeds; his finished obedience is the actual source salvation flows from, not merely its occasion. And "those who obey him" describes who the saved turn out to be, not the basis on which they are saved.
translation: And having been brought to completeness, he became, to all those who obey him, the source of eternal salvation.

label: Hebrews 5:10
text:
"Called" translates prosagoreuo, a verb used for the formal, public act of styling someone with a title — a solemn designation, not an offhand label.

God publicly proclaimed him high priest in the specific order of Melchizedek, and the timing matters: the title comes only after the discipline of suffering described in the verse before had run its full course.
translation: Publicly designated by God as a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

label: Hebrews 6:7–8
text:
The picture is agricultural: the same rain, falling repeatedly and generously, produces radically different results depending on the soil. One plot yields useful crops and receives blessing for it; the other, watered identically, yields only thorns and briers and ends up fit only for burning.

The point isn't a difference in what's given — the rain is identical — but a difference in the ground itself, in what each soil does with the same gift.
translation: For land that drinks in the rain that often falls on it, and produces vegetation useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless, and near to a curse — and its end is to be burned.

label: Hebrews 6:14
text:
The doubled phrasing — "blessing I will bless," "multiplying I will multiply" — reflects a Hebrew construction carried over into the Greek, where repeating a verb alongside its own root intensifies it.

It isn't redundancy; it's emphasis, the strongest way Hebrew had of saying it would happen without fail.
translation: Saying: Blessing, I will bless you; and multiplying, I will multiply you.

label: Hebrews 6:15
text:
"Obtained" is epitugchano, "to hit upon, attain" — and what Abraham actually attained in his lifetime was only the seed of the promise, not its full harvest.

Isaac's birth was the down payment, not the completed transaction; the promise's ultimate fulfillment reaches forward past Abraham's own lifetime.
translation: And so, having patiently waited, he obtained the promise.

label: Hebrews 6:17
text:
"Willing" is boulomai, marking a desire rooted in reasoned decision rather than a different word for desire rooted in feeling — God's oath is a considered resolve, not an emotional gesture. "Immutability" is ametathetos, built on metatithemi ("to transpose, change position") with a negating prefix — a related noun from the same root means "turncoat," so the point is pointed: God will not be a turncoat regarding his own promise.

"Confirmed" translates mesiteuo, "to act as mediator, to pledge oneself as surety" — from the same root as "mediator." God is pictured stepping in as his own guarantor, interposing himself between the promise and its heirs as witness to his own word.
translation: In this, God, wanting even more abundantly to show to the heirs of the promise the unchangeableness of his purpose, guaranteed it with an oath —

label: Hebrews 6:18
text:
"Things" translates pragma, from prasso ("to do, accomplish") — not vague objects but concrete, completed acts: the promise made and the oath sworn, both done deeds, both unchangeable. "Strong" is ischuros, describing indwelling strength like that of an army or a fortress — a bulwark, not a mild comfort.

And "fled for refuge" is katapheugo, the exact word used in the Greek Old Testament for the manslayer running to a city of refuge to escape the avenger of blood — an image the readers would already have known, of a fugitive with nowhere else to go, given one designated place of safety.
translation: So that, through two unchangeable acts in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to lay hold of the hope set before us.

label: Hebrews 6:20
text:
"Forerunner" introduces a concept entirely foreign to the old system — the Aaronic high priest went into the Holy of Holies as a substitute, standing in for people who themselves could never follow him there. Christ instead enters as one who blazes the trail, opening a way others will actually walk after him. The Greek carries no definite article before "forerunner," so translations that make the phrase sound like an already-familiar idea overstate the case slightly — this really is a new idea, introduced here for the first time.

And "Jesus" is, once again, simply the Greek form of the name for Israel's God — a quiet, constant reminder running through the letter that Israel's own Jehovah is the one who has gone ahead.
translation: Where Jesus, as a forerunner, entered on our behalf, having become a high priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.

label: Hebrews 7:2
text:
"Gave" is merizo, "to divide into portions, distribute" — Abraham's tithe was a deliberate, calculated apportioning, not an impulsive gift. The name Melchizedek itself breaks down to "king of righteousness," while "king of Salem" adds "king of peace."

Two titles stacked on top of each other, one drawn from his name, the other from the place he ruled, together sketching a portrait of righteousness and peace united in a single figure.
translation: To whom also Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything — his name meaning, first, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

label: Hebrews 7:3
text:
"Without father, without mother, without genealogy" describes an absence of record, not a miraculous birth — significant because Israel's priesthood ran entirely on documented lineage; a priest without a paper trail would ordinarily be disqualified. "Made like" translates aphomoioo, "to produce a facsimile" — the likeness lies in how Melchizedek's story is written, in what Scripture leaves out about him, not in some literal claim that he was himself eternal.

It's the silence of the record, not the man himself, that supplies the type. And the likeness specifically points to the Son as Son of God, not Son of Man — the eternal side of Christ's identity, since as Son of Man he plainly was born and did die.
translation: Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God — he remains a priest continually.

label: Hebrews 7:5
text:
The Levitical priests collected tithes strictly "according to the law" — under legal commandment, even from their own kinsmen descended from the same Abraham.

That's an important contrast the writer is setting up: compliance with a legal requirement carries no admission of personal inferiority on the part of those who pay it, which sharpens, by contrast, just how remarkable Abraham's voluntary tithe to Melchizedek was.
translation: And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment, according to the law, to collect tithes from the people — that is, from their brothers, though these have come from the loins of Abraham.

label: Hebrews 7:7
text:
"Dispute" translates antilogia, literally "word spoken against" — a word-for-word contradiction. The adjectives "lesser" and "greater" appear in the neuter gender in Greek, casting the statement in its widest, most general form.

Not this particular blessing only, but the principle itself, stated as an axiom nobody would think to argue against: the inferior is blessed by the superior, never the reverse.
translation: But beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.

label: Hebrews 7:13
text:
The writer's word choice for "another" tribe is heteros, "another of a different kind," rather than allos, "another of the same kind" — Christ doesn't simply belong to a different tribe than Levi's, he belongs to a tribe of an entirely different category, one with no connection whatsoever to altar service.

"Altar" itself is thusiasterion, specifically the altar where sacrificial victims were offered — not a generic word for altar, but the one tied directly to blood sacrifice, the very thing no member of Judah had any legal standing to perform.
translation: For he of whom these things are said belonged to a different kind of tribe, from which no one has ever attended at the altar.

label: Hebrews 7:14
text:
"Evident" is prodelos, "openly plain, obvious to everyone" — no dispute possible about the facts. "Sprang" translates anatello, the verb used for the sun or a star rising, or a cloud forming, or a plant coming up out of the ground — an image of emergence, of something breaking into visibility.

And "Lord" here is kurios, the standard Greek rendering of the divine name Jehovah throughout the Greek Old Testament — a title with weight, quietly asserting deity even while the sentence's actual subject is Christ's very human tribal origin.
translation: For it is plainly evident that our Lord has sprung from Judah — a tribe about which Moses said nothing regarding priests.

label: Hebrews 7:15
text:
"Far more evident" uses a different, stronger compound — katadelos, "thoroughly, unmistakably evident" — distinct from the plainer word used one verse earlier. That earlier word marked a simple historical fact, Christ's tribal origin.

This one marks something even more inescapable: the logical necessity, staring the reader in the face, that an entirely different kind of priesthood had to arise.
translation: And it is even more thoroughly evident that, after the likeness of Melchizedek, a different kind of priest arises.

label: Hebrews 7:16
text:
"Law" is nomos, a general norm or standard, narrowed here by entole, "commandment" — a specific precept, and that precept is called sarkinos, "fleshly": rules keyed to physical, bodily qualifications — the right family line, physical wholeness, ceremonial cleanness.

Against that stands akatalutos, "indissoluble" — built from luo ("loosen, dissolve") with a negating prefix — describing a life that cannot be broken apart into disunited pieces. Christ doesn't hold his priesthood by satisfying a checklist of physical requirements; he holds it by the sheer, unbreakable power of a life that even death couldn't dissolve.
translation: Who has become a priest, not according to the norm of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life.

label: Hebrews 7:17
text: This verse is simply the scriptural anchor for the claim just made — Psalm 110 again, cited to certify in Scripture's own words that the new priest's life, and therefore his priesthood, is permanent by divine testimony, not merely by the writer's own argument.
translation: For it is testified: You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.

label: Hebrews 7:22
text:
The writer's argument up to this point converges here: because God backed this priesthood with an oath — something never done for the Levitical line — Jesus becomes the guarantee, the pledge underwriting a better covenant.

The strength of the guarantee rests entirely on the strength of what backs it: an oath God cannot go back on.
translation: By as much, then, Jesus has become the pledge of a better covenant.

label: Hebrews 7:27
text:
The position of "daily" in the Greek sentence is doing careful work — it attaches to Christ's ongoing intercession, not to any need to repeat his sacrifice; his intercession runs daily, but the sacrifice behind it never needs renewing, unlike the Aaronic high priest's yearly repetition on the Day of Atonement. "Once for all" translates ephapax, a compound stressing finality — done, and done permanently.

And unlike every Aaronic priest, Christ never had to offer first for sins of his own before he could offer for anyone else's — there was nothing of his own to atone for.
translation: Who has no daily need, as those high priests did, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins and then for those of the people — for this he did once for all, when he offered up himself.

label: Hebrews 7:28
text:
"Weakness" here is astheneia, describing weakness as a defining, general characteristic rather than isolated lapses — the law's appointees are, by their very constitution, weak men.

Against that, the oath — which came later than the law and so supersedes it — appoints the Son, described with teleioo, "brought to completion, perfected": not a man patched up despite weakness, but one made complete, permanently, without that built-in defect.
translation: For the law appoints as high priests men who are, by nature, weak; but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son, made complete forever.

label: Hebrews 8:2
text: "Minister" translates *leitourgos* (leitourgos), built from an old word for "belonging to the people" plus *ergon* (ergon), "work" — it named someone in public office serving the state, and both the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament use it for service rendered to God as well as to people. Christ's priesthood is public, official work, not a private religious feeling. "Sanctuary" renders *ta hagia* (ta hagia), plural, "the holy places" — Christ ministers in the heavenly holies themselves. "Tabernacle" is simply the ordinary word for a tent. "True" is *alēthinos* (alethinos), and here it doesn't mean "genuine" as opposed to "fake" — it means "the real one" as opposed to a mere copy or representation. The earthly tent Moses built was never the counterfeit; it was the model. The tent the Lord himself pitched is the reality behind it, heaven's own Holy of Holies, and Christ's priesthood outranks Aaron's precisely because he serves there instead.
translation: A minister of the holy places, and of the tabernacle — the genuine one, which the Lord pitched, not man.

label: Hebrews 8:3
text: Every high priest exists to offer something — that is the job description. Priesthood without an offering is a contradiction in terms. So if Christ holds the office of high priest, the logic is airtight: he too must have something to present. The verse doesn't yet say what; it simply establishes the necessity, setting up the case the writer builds through the rest of the chapter that Christ's offering is himself.
translation: For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices; therefore it is necessary that this one also have something to offer.

label: Hebrews 8:4
text: The argument runs by elimination. The Levitical priesthood was fixed by the Law of Moses to men of Aaron's line functioning at an earthly altar — that post was already staffed, and staffed exclusively, by others, under legal right. If Christ's priestly work were an earthly function, he would have no priesthood left to hold, since the earthly slot belonged to a different order by law, not by merit. The very fact that he is a priest at all requires a sanctuary the Law never touched — a heavenly one.
translation: For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are those who offer the gifts according to law.

label: Hebrews 8:5
text:
"Example" is *hupodeigma* (hupodeigma), a rough sketch or outline suggestive of the real thing, and "shadow" is *skia* (skia) — literally a shadow cast by a solid object, with no substance of its own. A shadow proves something real is standing behind it, but it isn't that thing; it has no independent existence. That's the relationship the writer draws between the earthly tabernacle and the heavenly one: the Aaronic priests spent their whole careers serving a shadow, doing real work inside an unreal building.

The "better covenant" of verse 6 is said to be "established" — *nomotheteō* (nomotheteo), literally "to enact as law," sharing a root with *nomos* (nomos), "law." It isn't a handshake agreement; it's legislated, put on the books with full authority. Verse 7 then explains why a second covenant was needed at all: "sought" is *zēteō* (zeteo) in the imperfect tense, describing action that kept happening across a stretch of past time — not "a place was sought" once, but "a place kept on being sought." Dissatisfaction with the first covenant wasn't a later verdict handed down after the fact; it was live and ongoing while that covenant was still in force.

When God announces through Jeremiah that he will "make" a new covenant, the verb is *sunteleō* (sunteleo), "to bring to completion, to consummate" — a stronger word than the ordinary *poieō* (poieo), "to make," chosen to stress that this covenant finishes what the first one left undone. "Covenant" itself, *diathēkē* (diatheke), comes from *diatithēmi* (diatithemi) — *tithēmi* (tithemi), "to place," with a prefix carrying the sense "between" — literally something placed between two parties. The same noun does double duty later in the letter, naming both an arrangement between two and a will that only takes effect at the death of the one who made it.

Israel's failure is described with *emmenō* (emmeno), "to remain true to, abide by," which they didn't do, met by God's *ameleō* (ameleo) — *melō* (melo), "to care for," with a negating prefix, "to stop caring for." It marks a real shift, concern giving way to disregard. The promise that under the new covenant nobody will need a teacher uses a double negative in Greek, the strongest possible denial available — and it switches verbs for "know" partway through: *ginōskō* (ginosko), knowledge gained by being introduced to something you didn't know before, then *oida* (oida), simply and fully knowing. Everyone under the new covenant moves from having God explained to them, to just knowing him.

Finally, "old" is *palaios* (palaios), not *archaios* (archaios) — the difference between "worn out, obsolete" and merely "existing since long ago." The first covenant isn't retired for its age; it's retired for being used up. "Made old" is a perfect-tense verb, *palaioō* (palaioo), an action completed in the past whose effect still stands: the covenant was rendered obsolete the moment a new one was promised, and it has stayed obsolete ever since. "Waxeth old," *gēraskō* (gerasko), pictures the specific weakening that comes with age — decay headed toward an end, not neutral aging.
translation: They serve a sketch and shadow of the heavenly things — just as Moses, when about to construct the tabernacle, was warned: "See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain." But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is also mediator of a better covenant, one that has been enacted on the basis of better promises.

label: Hebrews 9:3
text: Exodus describes two veils in the tabernacle — one at the entrance to the Holy Place, a second separating the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies. The writer's phrase "the second veil" assumes his readers know that layout: pass through it, and you're standing where only the high priest ever stood, and only once a year.
translation: And behind the second veil, a tabernacle called the Holy of Holies.

label: Hebrews 9:4
text: Naming the golden censer among the furnishings of the Holy of Holies raises a real question, since the incense altar itself stood in the Holy Place, just outside the veil. The verb "had," *echō* (echo), doesn't have to mean "permanently contained" — it can mean simply "belonged to, pertained to." On the Day of Atonement a special golden censer, different from the one used the rest of the year, was carried past the veil by the high priest, filled with coals, so the incense cloud covered the mercy seat before he brought in the blood. That one-day use is likely what's in view. "Ark" is *kibōtos* (kibotos), simply "box" or "chest" — the same plain word used for any storage container, dignified here only by what it held: the tables of the law, and, on the tradition the writer follows, the jar of manna and Aaron's rod as well.
translation: having a golden censer, and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold, in which was a golden jar holding the manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.

label: Hebrews 9:5
text:
"Mercy seat" is *hilastērion* (hilasterion), the Greek Old Testament's word for the gold cover over the ark where atonement was made — the same word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25, usually rendered "propitiation." It's a word aimed at sin, not at anger. It doesn't describe an offering that talks an angry God down; it describes the removing of the barrier sin throws up between God and man, a covering-over that clears the way for fellowship. The blood sprinkled there stood between the broken law resting in the ark and the priest who approached on the people's behalf — exactly what Christ's blood does, permanently.

The next verse adds that the tabernacle's furnishings had been "prepared," *kataskeuazō* (kataskeuazo), in the perfect tense — set in place once, with the arrangement still standing — after which the priests entered the outer tent "continually," day after day, to carry out their service, *epiteleō* (epiteleo), a verb used elsewhere of completing a religious rite. The picture is one of routine access to the outer room set directly against the sealed, once-a-year access to the inner one.
translation: And above it, cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat — about which we cannot now speak in detail. These things having been set in place, the priests enter the first tent continually, performing the services.

label: Hebrews 9:7
text: The high priest's entry into the Holy of Holies was tightly restricted: once a year, alone, and never without blood. "Errors" translates *agnoēma* (agnoema), sin committed in ignorance or without full deliberation — even unintentional sin needed covering. "For" is *huper* (huper), the preposition of substitution, the same word used of one person dying in another's place. The blood wasn't a gesture; it stood in for the sinner, exactly as Christ's blood would.
translation: But into the second, only the high priest enters, once a year, and not without blood, which he offers on behalf of himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people.

label: Hebrews 9:8
text: The point here turns on timing, not vocabulary: as long as the tabernacle's two-room structure stood — an outer room anyone could enter, an inner room sealed off from everyone but the high priest, and him only once a year — the arrangement itself announced that the way into God's presence was not yet open. The building was the message. Its architecture, not a sermon, told Israel that direct access to God still lay in the future. When the veil tore at the cross, that architecture became obsolete on the spot, God's own comment on what had just been accomplished.
translation: The Holy Spirit making this clear: the way into the Holy Place had not yet been laid open, while the first tent was still standing.

label: Hebrews 9:9
text: "Figure" is *parabolē* (parabole) — literally something "thrown alongside" something else to explain it, the same root that gives us "parable." The tabernacle functioned exactly that way: a visual aid set alongside the reality, teaching by illustration rather than being the thing itself. "Perfect," *teleios* (teleios), doesn't mean sinless — it means complete, lacking nothing further needed to finish the job. No ritual, gift, or sacrifice under the old system could bring a worshiper's conscience to that state of completeness; at most it addressed the ceremony, never the conscience underneath it.
translation: This was a symbol for the present time, according to which gifts and sacrifices are being offered that are not able to make the worshiper complete as to his conscience.

label: Hebrews 9:10
text:
The old system's regulations rested, literally, "upon" (*epi*, epi) food and drink and various washings — its whole operating basis was bodily, not spiritual. "Meats" is *brōma* (broma), simply "food" in general, wider than the narrowed modern sense of animal flesh. These rules are called "carnal," *sarx* (sarx), "flesh" — meaning human, tied to the physical conditions of human life. They stood only "until the time of reformation" — *diorthōsis* (diorthosis), a word used elsewhere of straightening a crooked limb or setting a broken bone back into normal alignment. The old system wasn't evil; it was a splint, holding a fracture in place until the day it could be properly set right.

When Christ "came" as high priest, the verb is *paraginomai* (paraginomai), "to arrive on the scene, to come alongside" — the language of an advent, someone entering from outside rather than simply growing up within the system he was joining. He ministers "through," *dia* (dia), a greater tabernacle — the preposition of the means by which something is accomplished, making the sanctuary itself the channel of his priestly work. That tabernacle is explicitly not "of this creation," *ktisis* (ktisis) — it doesn't belong to the made, material universe at all.

"His own blood" uses *idios* (idios), not the ordinary possessive *autos* (autos) — *idios* marks personal, private, unique ownership, the same intensity John uses when he reports Jesus calling God his own Father in a sense no one else could claim. Christ entered "once for all," *ephapax* (ephapax), a single decisive act set against the priest's yearly repetition. And what he obtained he "found," *heuriskō* (heurisko) — not merely received, *lambanō* (lambano), but sought out and secured, the language of active procurement, matching "redemption," *lutrōsis* (lutrosis), from *lutron* (lutron), the ransom price paid to free a slave.

Ceremonial defilement is *koinoō* (koinoo), "to make common, unhallowed"; the cure is *hagiazō* (hagiazo), "to set apart for God" — restoration to a status, which is exactly the limit animal blood had. Christ, by contrast, offered himself "through eternal Spirit" — the Greek has no definite article before "Spirit," pointing not to an outside force acting on him but to his own eternal divine nature as the moving power behind the offering. That's what animals never brought to the altar: a will of their own, freely given.

"Mediator," *mesitēs* (mesites), names someone who stands between two parties to make or ratify an agreement — Christ standing between a holy God and sinful people, removing the obstacle between them. The writer then leans on the double sense of *diathēkē* (diatheke): the same word means both "covenant" and "will, testament," and a testament only takes legal effect once its maker has died. That's exactly why Christ's death was necessary to activate a covenant God had already promised — a will is only words on paper until the testator is gone.

Everything connected to the old covenant's inauguration — the book, the people, the tabernacle and its vessels — was sprinkled with blood, because without blood shed there is no forgiveness. Even heaven's own sanctuary needed cleansing before Christ could enter it, though with a better sacrifice than animal blood could supply. The earthly tabernacle is called *antitypon* (antitupon), a "corresponding type" of the heavenly one, while the heavenly is called *alēthinos* (alethinos) — genuinely, fully what the earthly one only pointed toward.
translation: These were only regulations for the body — foods and drinks and various washings — imposed until the time for setting things right. Not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, he entered once for all into the Holy Place, having sought out and secured eternal redemption.

label: Hebrews 9:26
text:
The phrase rendered "in the end of the world" is literally "at the consummation of the ages" — not the world's final moment but history's ages reaching their intended completion, the point everything before had been building toward. "Appeared" is *phaneroō* (phaneroo) in the perfect passive: not simply "he appeared and the moment passed," but "he has been manifested" — an action finished that leaves a permanent, standing result. One sacrifice, offered once, settles the matter for every age it touches; that's the whole point of contrasting it with sacrifices that had to be repeated endlessly because none of them actually finished anything.

That logic carries straight into the next chapter, where the Law is said to hold only a "shadow," *skia* (skia), of the good things to come, not the "image," *eikōn* (eikon), of the realities themselves. A shadow is a vague outline cast by something solid — useful for telling you a shape is there, useless for showing you what it actually looks like. An *eikōn* is a true likeness, faithful in its details. That's why the sacrifices "make perfect," *teleioō* (teleioo), no one — not because they were badly performed, but because a shadow, however many times you retrace it, never becomes the object that cast it. The repetition itself was the tell: something that actually finished the job wouldn't need to be re-offered every year.
translation: But now, once, at the consummation of the ages, he has been manifested for the putting away of sin through the sacrifice of himself. For the law, holding only a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the realities, is never able, by the same sacrifices continually offered year after year, to make complete those who approach.

label: Hebrews 10:2
text: The logic of the verse is a kind of test: if the yearly sacrifices had actually finished the job of cleansing, the ritual would have stopped, because a worshipper who is truly clean carries no more consciousness of sin needing to be dealt with. The fact that the offering had to be repeated every single year is itself the proof that nothing final had happened there — the problem persisted, so the remedy kept being reapplied. That doesn't mean Old Testament believers were left stranded in the meantime; a worshipper who brought his sacrifice in genuine faith, trusting God to one day provide the real payment for sin, was reckoned righteous on that basis, in full, from the moment he believed. The repetition exposed the limits of the animal blood itself, not the sincerity of the faith it was meant to picture.
translation: Would they not then have stopped being offered, since the worshippers, having once been cleansed, would no longer be carrying even one troubled conscience about sins?

label: Hebrews 10:3
text: "Remembrance" renders *anamnesis* (anamnesis), a noun meaning "a calling back to mind" rather than a removal. Each year's Day of Atonement didn't erase guilt from the worshippers' memory — paradoxically, it revived it. The very ceremony meant to deal with sin ended up rehearsing it annually, which told the worshippers, whether they admitted it to themselves or not, that the sacrifice hadn't actually settled the account.
translation: But in them there kept occurring, year after year, a calling back to mind of sins.

label: Hebrews 10:4
text: The claim needs no elaborate defense because the mismatch is self-evident: an animal's blood is a physical substance, and sin is a moral offense against God. There is no natural bridge between those two categories, and no quantity of repeated animal sacrifice manufactures one. That is precisely why the whole system could only ever point forward to something else — it was never built to close the gap on its own.
translation: For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

label: Hebrews 10:6
text: This isn't a blanket statement that God despised the Levitical offerings. The Israelites who brought them were obeying a command He Himself had given, and their obedience genuinely pleased Him. What He took no pleasure in was the offerings' capacity to function as an actual payment for sin — as a transaction meant to settle guilt, they accomplished nothing, however faithfully they were carried out.
translation: In whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin you took no pleasure.

label: Hebrews 10:7
text: "It stands written of me" reaches back to Scripture already on record — the Messiah's assignment wasn't drawn up after the sacrificial system proved inadequate; it was there in the text from the start, waiting for Him to step into it. The phrase functions almost like a legal citation: the terms were filed long before the moment of fulfillment arrived. When Messiah does step in, the passage continues, He does more than simply add a better sacrifice alongside the old ones — He sets aside the first order of things specifically to make room for the second, so that what could never satisfy God's will gives way to what actually does.
translation: Then I said, Behold, I have come — in the roll of the book it stands written of me — to do your will, O God.

label: Hebrews 10:10
text:
"Sanctified" translates *hagiazo* (hagiazo), "to set apart for God" — here describing not a gradual ethical improvement but the once-for-all placement of a believing sinner into the status of one who belongs to God, with everything that status carries. The Greek underlines the permanence of it: "we are sanctified" pairs a perfect participle with a present-tense verb, a construction built specifically to say that the state was entered decisively and continues without interruption. "Once for all" belongs with "the offering of the body of Jesus Christ" — a single, unrepeatable act accomplishing what years of repeated offerings never could.

The verses that follow press the same contrast physically. Every Levitical priest is pictured standing, day after day, offering the same sacrifices that never actually remove sin — the posture is the point: nobody sits down in the middle of unfinished work. Messiah, by contrast, sat down after His one offering, and stayed seated. A finished sacrifice gets a seated priest; an unfinished one keeps its priest on his feet indefinitely.
translation: By which will we have been made holy, and stand holy still, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, once for all.

label: Hebrews 10:16–18
text:
The old covenant carved its law onto stone tablets handed down from outside. The new covenant, quoted here from Jeremiah, has God writing the same law directly onto mind and heart — an internalized instinct rather than an external code to consult. The second marker of the new covenant is even more striking: God says He will no longer remember the sins and lawless acts at all. Once that is true, nothing is left for a sacrifice to do — the writer's argument closes right there: no more remembrance of sin means no more need of an offering for it.

The road into God's presence that follows is called, in the Greek, *prosphatos* (prosphatos) — built from a root meaning "near" combined with the word behind "to kill." Its plain sense is "freshly slain," not merely "new" the way we'd use the word today. It's a road opened by a killing and sprinkled in blood, set against the older road to the tabernacle's mercy seat, itself opened only by animal blood but now superseded. The curtain that once blocked entry is identified with Messiah's own body — torn, as the veil was torn, so that what had barred access now stands open.

The priest who leads the way in is described in the Greek not as one compound title but as two separate words: "a priest, a great one" — the greatness gets its own emphasis, distinct from the office itself. Believers are told to approach with a heart called *alethinos* (alethinos), "genuine" — the kind of heart that actually matches what it claims to be — sprinkled clean and washed, borrowing the picture of a priest ceremonially prepared before entering to serve.

Holding on to that confession gets its own vocabulary too. "Hold fast" is *katecho* (katecho), "to hold down" — a grip firm enough to master what it holds, not a loose grasp. "Wavering" is *aklines* (aklines), built from the verb "to lean" with a negating prefix attached — literally "not leaning," the picture of something built to stay upright rather than tip backward under pressure. And believers are told to give each other *katanoeo* (katanoeo), sustained, attentive observation, aimed at stirring up love and good works — the same root that gives English "paroxysm" describes that stirring: a deliberate provocation, meant here in the best possible sense.
translation: This is the covenant that I will decree for them after those days, says the Lord: I will keep putting my laws upon their hearts, and upon their minds I will keep inscribing them; and their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more, not ever. Now where release from these has been granted, there is no longer any offering for sin.

label: Hebrews 10:25
text:
"Forsaking" is *egkataleipo* (egkataleipo), "to let down, to abandon" — stronger than simply missing a meeting; it pictures dropping something you had been holding up. "Assembling together" is *episunagoge* (episunagoge), built on the same root that gives us "synagogue" (a going-together), with an added preposition that sharpens it toward the actual, concrete gathering rather than the abstract idea of a congregation. Some among the readers, under pressure, had quietly begun dropping out; the exhortation runs the other direction — show up for each other, and do it more, not less, as the day visibly draws nearer.

The sin described next is qualified by *hekousios* (hekousios), "voluntarily, of one's own accord" — set in deliberate contrast to sins committed out of ignorance or weakness. The Greek present tense behind "if we go on sinning" points to a settled, habitual course rather than a single lapse. And the knowledge in view isn't the bare, surface-level *gnosis* (gnosis); it's *epignosis* (epignosis), a fuller, more personal grasp of the truth — someone who had genuinely understood, not merely heard, and turned away with eyes wide open.

What is left for such a person is only "a fearful expectation of judgment" — closer to "a kind of dreadful looking-for" — because the one available sacrifice has already been consciously rejected. The comparison then drops back to the Mosaic law itself: a person who set that law aside died without mercy, on the testimony of two or three witnesses. If that was the penalty under the lesser system, the argument presses, what penalty fits the far greater offense described next?

Three actions define that greater offense, one against each person of the Godhead: trampling the Son of God underfoot, treating His blood as ordinary, and insulting the Spirit of grace. "Ordinary" renders *koinos* (koinos), whose basic sense is "shared by all, common property" — the direct opposite of what is set apart for sacred use. To call the covenant blood *koinos* is to strip it of any special worth and treat it as no different from anyone else's. That is the substance of the apostasy this passage is warning against — not ignorance, but a deliberate downgrade of what deserves the highest reverence.
translation: Not abandoning the gathering of ourselves together, as the custom of some is, but continually encouraging one another — and all the more as you see the day drawing near.

label: Hebrews 10:30
text: The certainty behind the warning rests on God's own word, not on a threat of petty payback. "Vengeance" can mislead a modern reader — the underlying idea is the full, impartial execution of justice, giving every party exactly what is due. The citation draws two lines from the Song of Moses: one declaring that the administering of justice belongs to God alone, the other that the Lord will judge His own people. Together they rule out any assumption that covenant privilege buys an exemption — belonging to God's people places a person squarely under His judgment, never beyond it.
translation: For we know the one who said, Justice belongs to me — I will repay. And again, The Lord will judge his people.

label: Hebrews 10:31
text: The statement stands as a summary verdict on everything just argued: someone who has trampled the Son, cheapened His blood, and insulted the Spirit has stepped out from under grace and directly into the path of God's own justice. Nothing abstract is meant by it — the "living God" is not a passive judge but an active one, and nothing made by Him escapes His hands.
translation: It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

label: Hebrews 10:33
text: "Made a spectacle" translates *theatrizo* (theatrizo), the root behind our word "theater" — to be put on public display for contempt, the very word later used to describe Christians literally thrown to wild animals in the Roman arena. Here the arena was social rather than literal: reproach and pressure aimed at those who had left the synagogue system for the new covenant. "Afflictions" in this verse is a different word than the one used just before it — *thlipsis* (thlipsis), which pictures pressure applied from outside, a squeezing. The persecution reached further than belief alone: it extended to anyone who stood in solidarity with the persecuted. The word for that solidarity, *koinonia* (koinonia), means active partnership — these believers shared materially in others' suffering, and were targeted for the sharing as much as for the faith itself.
translation: On the one hand, you were being made a public spectacle through both insults and pressures; on the other, you were making yourselves partners with those who were being treated this way.

label: Hebrews 10:34
text: The "partnership" of the previous verse gets defined here in concrete terms: sympathy toward those in prison, and a striking response to having their own property seized. "Accepted" is *prosdechomai* (prosdechomai), "to receive to oneself" — a word implying willing acceptance rather than mere passive endurance. What made joy possible in the face of real loss was the knowledge of a possession that couldn't be confiscated: an asset outside the reach of any seizure, permanent where the earthly one was not.
translation: For you sympathized with those in bonds, and you accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy, knowing that you yourselves possess something better, and one that continues to remain.

label: Hebrews 10:35
text: "Confidence" translates *parresia* (parresia), built from the words for "all" and "speech" — literally the freedom to say everything, unguarded and unreserved. It names the bold, unashamed posture these believers had already shown under real pressure. The exhortation isn't to acquire some new virtue but to stop discarding one they already had — and the reason given is blunt: that confidence carries a payoff worth protecting.
translation: So do not throw away your confidence, which carries a great reward.

label: Hebrews 10:36
text: "Receive" is *komizo* (komizo), which means more than simply obtaining something — it pictures carrying an item away for one's own use and benefit, the way one collects what is owed. "Patience" translates *hupomone* (hupomone), built from "to remain" plus "under" — literally staying put beneath a weight rather than trying to escape it. The exhortation isn't to feel patient; it's to stay under the pressure without bolting, because the promised reward only reaches the one still standing there when it arrives.
translation: For you have need of endurance — of remaining under — so that, having done the will of God, you may carry away the promise for yourselves.

label: Hebrews 10:37
text: The wording intensifies the wait rather than shortening it: not just "a little while" but something closer to "a very little — however little — while," the smallness doubled for emphasis. The line draws on Habakkuk's prophecy of a coming vision that would not fail, language already applied by Jewish interpreters to the Messiah's arrival before this writer picked it up the same way.
translation: For yet a very little — how very little — while, and the one who is coming will come, and will not delay.

label: Hebrews 10:39
text: The sentence opens with an emphatic personal pronoun, drawing a hard line between the writer's own company and the hypothetical person just described: "But we — we are not of the shrinking-back kind." Both "those who draw back" and "those who believe" are phrased in the Greek as descriptions of a class of person, not as isolated, one-time acts — this is about which kind of person someone fundamentally is, not a single bad decision made under strain. "Destruction" translates *apoleia* (apoleia), the same word used elsewhere for utter, final ruin — not a setback but the loss of the soul itself.
