Set against it is the "preserving of the soul," the outcome that belongs, by nature, to the believing kind.
translation: But as for us, we are not of the shrinking-back kind, who shrink back to destruction, but of the believing kind, who believe unto the preserving of the soul.

label: Hebrews 11:2
text: "Obtained a good report" renders *emartyrēthēsan* (emartyrethesan), the aorist passive of *martyreō* (martyreo), "to bear witness." The direction of the verb matters: this isn't the elders testifying to something, it's witness being borne to them — God himself put his stamp of approval on their lives. "By it" translates *en tautē* (en taute), a phrase that sits on the border between two Greek cases: it can mean "in the sphere of" faith and "by means of" faith at once, so faith is named as both the arena these people lived in and the tool that got results for them. And "elders" (not the more usual "fathers") is a deliberately broad label, reaching for every Old Testament saint the chapter is about to parade past.
translation: For by means of this the elders had witness borne to them.

label: Hebrews 11:3
text:
"Understand" translates *noeō* (noeo), the verb for perceiving with the reflective mind rather than the eye. In the New Testament it's never used of plain physical sight — it names the mental grasp that follows seeing and draws a conclusion from it. Faith, in this verse, isn't opposed to reason; it's reason correctly applied to what's in front of you, concluding a Maker from what's made.

"Worlds" is *aiōn* (aion), not the ordinary word for the physical globe. *Aiōn* reaches past matter to include the ages themselves — the created order understood as space and time together, both of them God's product rather than a backdrop he happened to build inside of.

"Framed" is *katartizō* (katartizo), the verb used for equipping or fitting something out for the purpose it's meant to serve — a craftsman assembling parts so the whole works as intended. The universe wasn't just produced; it was outfitted, tuned to its purpose.

And the "word" by which it was framed is *hrēma* (hrema), the word for an uttered statement, not *logos* (logos), the title John gives the Son in his Gospel's opening verse. This verse is about God's spoken command bringing the ages into being, not about the person of the Word. The visible, in other words, came out of the invisible — which is exactly why grasping it takes faith and not observation.
translation: By faith we perceive that the ages have been fitted together by the spoken word of God, so that what is seen has not come to exist out of things that are visible.

label: Hebrews 11:5
text:
"Translated" is *metatithēmi* (metatithemi), a compound built on the verb "to place" plus a prefix meaning change — literally "to transpose," to put one thing where another had been. The same word describes moving Jacob's bones to a new burial site and swapping one legal arrangement for another elsewhere in the New Testament. Applied to Enoch, it pictures a straight substitution: heaven put in the place earth had occupied, with no interval of death between the two.

The verse doesn't actually credit Enoch with faith to be translated. God did the translating because Enoch's life pleased him, and it was faith that produced that life in the first place. Genesis' own commentary on the man is simply that he walked with God — ongoing, close company, the kind faith alone sustains.

"Had witness borne to him" sits in the perfect tense — not a single compliment paid once, but a testimony still standing on record. The verdict on Enoch's life was settled and filed before the transfer to heaven ever happened.
translation: By faith Enoch was transferred, so that he did not see death, and he was not found, because God had transferred him. For before his transfer, he had been attested — the record still stands — that he was one who pleased God.

label: Hebrews 11:6
text:
The infinitive behind "to please" is aorist, and here that marks a flat, timeless axiom rather than one occasion — without faith, pleasing God isn't merely difficult, it's impossible, no exceptions carved out.

Two different verbs sit behind the sentence's two English "is"-es. The first, that God "is," comes from the plain verb of existence: he simply exists. The second, that he "is a rewarder," comes from *ginomai* (ginomai), the verb of becoming — not a static fact to assent to, but an outcome God proves true in the seeker's own experience. Faith isn't stopping at "God exists"; it's trusting that he will show himself faithful to the one who comes to him.

"Diligently seek" carries a prefix that sharpens the ordinary verb for seeking into searching something out, tracking it to the end rather than glancing at it once. Faith keeps looking.
translation: But without faith it is impossible to please him at all, for the one who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he proves himself a rewarder to those who are earnestly searching him out.

label: Hebrews 11:7
text:
"Moved with fear" softens a word that isn't about fright at all. *Eulabeomai* (eulabeomai) means to act with reverent caution — the wary, careful respect of a man taking seriously a warning about something he can't yet see. Noah wasn't spooked into building; he was sobered into it.

"Prepared" is *kataskeuazō* (kataskeuazo), the verb for equipping and outfitting something for use, not merely nailing boards together. Noah didn't just build a hull, he fitted it out to actually keep his household alive. "Ark" (*kibōtos*, kibotos) is the same word later used for the ark of the covenant — a wooden chest built to carry something precious safely through danger.

*Kosmos* (kosmos), "world," can mean either the physical earth or the human race, and the ambiguity is worth keeping rather than resolving: Noah's faith condemned both at once — it announced coming judgment on the earth itself, and by sheer contrast it exposed the unbelief of everyone around him. The righteousness he's said to have "become heir of" is righteousness in conduct, the fruit his faith produced in a life actually lived, not the righteousness that first declares a sinner right with God.
translation: By faith Noah, having been warned about things not yet seen, with reverent caution equipped an ark for the saving of his household, through which he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes according to faith.

label: Hebrews 11:8
text:
"When he was called" translates a present participle running alongside the main verb "obeyed" — the two actions overlap in the Greek. Abraham's obedience wasn't a response that came later; it happened in the very moment of the call, obedience and summons landing together.

"Not knowing" whither he went uses *epistamai* (epistamai), not the ordinary verbs for knowing facts. *Epistamai* is about fixing the mind's attention on something. So this isn't ignorance Abraham stumbled into — it's that he refused to let the unknown destination occupy his thoughts. He didn't need the itinerary to obey the command.
translation: By faith Abraham, at the very time he was being called, obeyed by going out to a place he was going to receive as an inheritance, and he went out without fixing his mind on where he was going.

label: Hebrews 11:9
text:
"Sojourned" is *paroikeō* (paroikeo), the standard word for a resident alien — someone living inside a community's borders without a citizen's rights. Paired with it is the preposition *eis* (eis), which ordinarily marks motion toward a place rather than settled rest. The grammar itself does the work: Abraham moved into the land, and then stayed there as a permanent outsider — at home nowhere and everywhere at once.

"Strange" (*allotria*, allotria) simply means "belonging to another." Abraham lived in the very land God had promised him as though it were someone else's property, housed in tents (*skēnē*, skene), the shelter of a man who expects to move again. Isaac and Jacob are named beside him because between the three of them they cover the entire span of that unsettled life in Canaan, all three still waiting on the one promise.
translation: By faith he went and settled as a foreigner without citizen's rights in the land of the promise, as in a land belonging to another, living in tents together with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of that same promise.

label: Hebrews 11:10
text:
Both "city" and "foundations" carry the definite article in the Greek — not a city, but the city, the one with the foundations. Abraham had a specific destination in view, not a vague heavenly notion.

The two words for God's role here, "builder" (*technitēs*, technites) and "maker" (*dēmiourgos*, demiourgos), are trade-guild language. *Technitēs* is the skilled architect who designs; *dēmiourgos* originally named a workman who builds for the public — for a whole community, not a private patron. Abraham wasn't waiting on real estate. He was waiting on a city God had designed and built for a people.
translation: For he was continually looking forward to the city that has the foundations, the city whose architect and builder is God.

label: Hebrews 11:11
text:
The intensive pronoun "herself" carries real weight — this is the very Sarah who had laughed at the promise in disbelief, now singled out as the one who received power to conceive. Faith didn't erase her history of doubt; it overtook it.

The phrase behind "to conceive seed" uses *katabolē* (katabole), literally "a throwing down" — the same word used elsewhere for the founding of the world. It's blunt, physical language for conception, but the shared vocabulary links Sarah's body to the same divine capability that laid the world's foundations: the God who founds worlds can found a family in a womb long past its season.

Her faith rests on a specific judgment about God's character. "Considered him faithful" is a verb of reasoned conclusion, not a feeling — she weighed the evidence of who God is and decided he could be trusted to keep his word, whatever her own body told her.
translation: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive offspring, even though she was past the proper age, because she had judged him faithful who had made the promise.

label: Hebrews 11:12
text:
"Sprang" renders an aorist passive of *gennaō* (gennao), "to beget" — one decisive event, not a slow buildup. From a single man an entire nation was born, and the writer underlines just how unlikely that was by adding the emphatic phrase "and that too," practically leaning on the word "one."

That one man is described with a perfect passive participle usually rendered "as good as dead" — the verb means "rendered dead, deadened," and the perfect tense marks this as a settled condition rather than a passing low point: Abraham's body had, for every practical purpose, already given out for fathering children. Paul reaches for the identical participle describing Abraham's body in Romans 4:19.

"Innumerable" stacks a negating prefix onto the verb "to count" — not simply a great many, but a multitude that has outrun counting, matched against the writer's two pictures of scale: the stars overhead and the sand at the sea's edge.
translation: And therefore there were born, from one man — and him as good as dead — descendants like the stars of heaven in number, and like the sand along the seashore, beyond counting.

label: Hebrews 11:13
text:
"In faith" is *kata pistin* (kata pistin), literally "according to faith" — these people didn't merely happen to have faith when death came; they died under faith's rule, governed by it rather than by sight.

"Embraced" translates *aspazomai* (aspazomai), the ordinary verb for greeting or waving at someone. The picture is of sailors saluting a coastline they can see on the horizon but haven't yet reached — they saw the fulfillment only from a distance and hailed it as certain, without ever setting foot on it.

Calling themselves "strangers and pilgrims" wasn't self-pity; it was a confession they made willingly, accepting a homeless life now because faith had already secured them a home later.
translation: These all died governed by faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from a distance and having waved them a greeting, and having confessed that they were strangers and temporary residents on the earth.

label: Hebrews 11:14
text:
"Say" is a present participle, *legontes* (legontes) — not something said once, but something kept on saying, a settled confession repeated as a matter of course. Their admission of homelessness wasn't a passing remark; it was their standing testimony about themselves.

"Fatherland" (*patris*, patris) is built directly on the word for father — not merely "a country," but the ancestral home that belongs to one's own line. And "seeking" carries an intensifying prefix that sharpens the ordinary verb into an active, deliberate search. They weren't drifting toward somewhere vague; they were pursuing a specific home they knew was theirs by right.
translation: For those who keep saying such things make it plain that they are earnestly seeking a fatherland.

label: Hebrews 11:15
text:
"Been mindful" renders an imperfect verb — not one backward glance but a habitual, ongoing remembering. The logic runs: if they had kept dwelling on the country they'd left, the door back would have stood open the whole time.

"Opportunity" is *kairos* (kairos), not the word for clock-time but for a fitting, seizable occasion. Turning back was a live option available to them at every stage, not a door slammed shut behind them. Their not returning was a continual choice against a continual possibility — which is exactly what makes it evidence of faith rather than mere circumstance.
translation: And if indeed they had kept remembering that country from which they had come out, they would have kept having opportunity to turn back.

label: Hebrews 11:16
text:
"Called" translates *epikaleisthai* (epikaleisthai), a compound that means specifically "to be surnamed" — adding a name onto one someone already bears. God isn't merely willing to be associated with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; he takes their names onto his own as a surname he's glad to wear — "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."

"Prepared" is a simple aorist, a completed and settled act. God has already built the city these patriarchs were reaching for, and that finished provision is the very ground given for why he isn't ashamed to carry their name. The relationship isn't tentative on his side.
translation: But now, as the case stands, they are reaching for a better country, that is, a heavenly one. That is why God is not ashamed to be called by their name, as their God — for he prepared a city for them.

label: Hebrews 11:17–19
text:
The verb behind "offered up" stands in the perfect tense while "being tested" runs alongside it as a present participle — grammatically, Abraham had already offered Isaac before the test ever reached its conclusion. The sacrifice was complete in his will well before any hand stopped his; the perfect tense marks it as a settled, finished act of the heart, not a last-second reversal.

Isaac is called "only begotten" (*monogenēs*, monogenes) even though Abraham had another son in Ishmael. The word marks him as unique with respect to the promise — the one specific son through whom the line was to run, irreplaceable for that purpose whether or not he was literally the only child.

"Received him back in a figure" (*en parabolē*, en parabole) signals that the resurrection in view here was symbolic, not literal — Isaac never actually died. The ram substituted in the thicket enacted death and restoration in Isaac's place, a parable acted out, and Abraham's reasoning that God could raise the dead proved sound within that acted picture, long before it was tested on the real thing at an empty tomb.
translation: By faith Abraham, while being tested, had already offered up Isaac — yes, he who had received the promises was offering up his one-of-a-kind son, the one about whom it had been said, In Isaac shall your seed be called — having reasoned that God was able to raise him even from among the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.

label: Hebrews 11:20
text: The Greek carries a small "and" that some English versions drop: "by faith, and that concerning things to come, Isaac blessed..." The extra word throws emphasis onto the blessing's reach — this wasn't a wish for the next harvest, it reached forward to events neither son would live to see fulfilled.
translation: By faith, and that regarding things still to come, Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau.

label: Hebrews 11:21
text: *Hekaston* (hekastos), "each," rather than a vague "both," marks Jacob's blessing as two distinct, deliberate acts — he blessed Manasseh and Ephraim individually, discerning between them, much as he had already shown discernment in placing the younger son ahead of the elder. The detail "leaning on the top of his staff" reproduces the Greek Old Testament's rendering of Genesis 47:31, where the unpointed Hebrew consonants could be read either "staff" or "bed" depending on which vowels were supplied. The Septuagint translators chose "staff," and the writer to the Hebrews simply follows that established Greek wording rather than working back to the Hebrew himself. Whichever object is actually meant, the picture stands: a dying man too weak to stand upright, still bowing in worship.
translation: By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each one of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff.

label: Hebrews 11:22
text: "Made mention" translates *emnēmoneusen* (mnēmoneuō), "to call to mind, to remember" — but here the memory runs forward rather than back. Joseph is dying in Egypt with no exodus yet in sight; his faith consists in remembering God's ancient promise to Abraham clearly enough to stake his own burial arrangements on it centuries in advance. The instruction concerning his bones, fulfilled only when Joshua finally carried them into Canaan, is the tangible proof: a man ordering his own skeleton moved because he trusted a promise he would never live to see kept.
translation: By faith Joseph, when he was coming to his end, called to mind the exodus of the sons of Israel, and gave command concerning his bones.

label: Hebrews 11:23
text: "Proper" translates *asteion* (asteios), a word that originally described someone with the polish of the city — "urbane, refined" — before it broadened to mean simply "beautiful, comely." The phrase is a dative of respect: the child was comely with respect to God, meaning in God's own estimation, not merely his parents' fond judgment. Stephen uses the identical word of the infant Moses in Acts 7:20. "Commandment" renders *diatagma* (diatagma), a formal royal edict rather than an informal directive — Pharaoh's order carried the full weight of state law, which makes the parents' three-month concealment a calculated act of civil disobedience grounded in a higher allegiance than the throne.
translation: By faith Moses, after he was born, was hidden three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was comely; and they did not fear the king's edict.

label: Hebrews 11:24–26
text: "Choosing" is an aorist middle participle — a single decisive act of the will, not a gradual drift away from Egypt. The "pleasures of sin" Moses walked away from translate *apolausin* (apolausis), a word for full, satisfied enjoyment rather than crude vice; the phrase covers the ambition and refined comforts available to him in Pharaoh's court, not merely sensual indulgence. "He esteemed" translates *hēgēsamenos* (hēgeomai), the language of calculation and weighing — an aorist that pictures Moses doing the math once and reckoning Christ's reproach worth more than Egypt's treasure. "He had respect unto" renders *aphorōn* (aphoraō), a compound verb meaning literally "to look away from" one thing in order to fix the eyes on another; it is present tense, a sustained, ongoing gaze, not a single glance. And "recompense" is *misthapodosian* (misthapodosia), built from *misthos* ("wages") and the verb "to pay back" — not a gift graciously bestowed but a wage owed, the debt God guarantees to settle.
translation: By faith Moses, when he had become great, refused to be called a son of Pharaoh's daughter, having chosen rather to be mistreated together with the people of God than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin, having counted the reproach of the Messiah greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt; for he was continually looking away to the reward.

label: Hebrews 11:27
text: "He endured" translates *ekarteresen* (kartereō), built on *karteros*, "strong, steadfast" — the verb pictures holding out with a firm grip. The tense is a constative aorist: it scoops up all forty years in Midian into a single summary snapshot of persistent faith rather than narrating them year by year. The apparent tension with Exodus 2:15, where fear drives Moses out of Egypt, dissolves once the two fears in view are distinguished: one fear — of being exposed as the Egyptian's killer — sent him running; a different fear he refused to feel, cowering before Pharaoh's continued wrath once his flight had already declared him committed to his own people. "As seeing" is a present participle, not a single glance but a sustained, ongoing gaze fixed on the invisible God — the thing that kept him steady through four decades of obscurity.
translation: By faith he left Egypt behind, not fearing the anger of the king; for he held out with a steadfast grip, as one continually seeing him who is invisible.

label: Hebrews 11:28
text: "Kept" translates a perfect tense of *poieō*, "to make, institute" — *pepoiēken* — and the perfect tense is the whole point: it doesn't just report a past founding, it insists the significance of what Moses instituted still held at the moment of writing. The Passover ritual itself was always temporary, a shadow due to expire once the reality it pointed to arrived; but as a picture of Christ's sacrifice, its meaning remained fully in force for the letter's first readers. "Sprinkling" is *proschysin* (proschysis), from a verb meaning "to pour toward" or "dash against" — describing a forceful action rather than a light mist, closer to pouring blood against a doorpost than dabbing it on with a brush.
translation: By faith he has instituted the Passover and the pouring out of the blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn should not touch them.

label: Hebrews 11:29
text: The commentary tradition has little to add here, but the Greek text itself repays a glance. "Passed through" is *diebēsan* (diabainō), an aorist that treats the whole crossing as one accomplished act rather than a slow process. "Taking a trial of it" (*peiran labontes*) is a vivid idiom — the Egyptians didn't simply attempt the same crossing, they "took a taste" or "made an experiment" of the sea, as though testing whether it would hold for them too. It did not. "Were drowned" translates *katepothēsan* (katapinō), "to gulp down, swallow" — the sea doesn't merely drown the pursuers in this picture, it swallows them whole.
translation: By faith they passed through the Red Sea as through dry land; and when the Egyptians attempted the same, they were swallowed up.

label: Hebrews 11:30
text: Another bare entry, but two grammatical facts stand out. "Fell" (*epesan*, from piptō) is a plain aorist — one completed collapse, not a gradual crumbling. "Having been encircled" (*kyklōthenta*, from kykloō) is an aorist passive participle: the walls did not fall because Israel stormed them, but only after they had first been marched around. The order of the Greek clause preserves the logic of Joshua 6 — circling in obedience, faith exercised in the waiting, and only then the collapse.
translation: By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after they had been encircled for seven days.

label: Hebrews 11:31
text: "Believed not" translates *apeithēsasin* (apeitheō), not the ordinary word for unbelief but one built on the idea of disobedience — the sin of Jericho's residents was not simple doubt but a refusal to act on news of Israel's God that had already reached them. Rahab's contrasting verb, "received," is *dexamenē* (dechomai), the word for welcoming a guest as a friend rather than merely admitting a stranger into one's house — she did not just let the spies in, she took their side. "With peace" underscores the same point: she received them without enmity or treachery, at genuine risk to herself.
translation: By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish along with those who were disobedient, having welcomed the spies as friends, in peace.

label: Hebrews 11:32
text: The writer breaks off the roll call with a rhetorical question built on a striking verb: *epileipsei* (epileipō), "to fail, run short, give out" — the word used of a spring running dry or supplies giving out. Time itself, he says, will fail him before the stories do; the participle *diēgoumenon* (diēgeomai), "narrating, recounting in detail," pictures him cut off mid-story, not for want of material but for want of hours. The six names that follow — Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel — are simply piled up with no interest in chronological or moral ranking; the effect wanted is sheer accumulated weight of testimony.
translation: And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I go on narrating about Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David also, and Samuel, and the prophets.

label: Hebrews 11:33
text: "Subdued" translates *katēgōnisanto* (katagōnizomai), a compound built on the same root as our word "agony" — literally "to fight down, wrestle to the ground." It is the language of a desperate, close-quarters struggle, not an easy walkover, and it fits kings like David wrestling entire kingdoms into submission. "Wrought righteousness" pairs these conquests with just governance: the phrase has in view not merely private virtue but the public exercise of power, faith showing itself in these men by binding conquest to justice rather than to tyranny.
translation: Who through faith wrestled down kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained the fulfillment of promises, shut the mouths of lions.

label: Hebrews 11:34
text: The list piles up short, punchy aorists with no connecting particles — a rhetorical burst rather than a smooth sentence. "Quenched the power of fire" uses *dynamin* (dynamis) in its raw sense of "force, violence," not abstract potency. "Escaped the edge of the sword" is literally "escaped the mouths of the sword" (*stomata machairēs*) — the same word used for a beast's mouth, picturing the blade as something that devours rather than merely cuts. "Out of weakness were made strong" is a passive, *edynamōthēsan* (dynamoō) — strength given, not achieved, sharing its root with *dynamis* above. "Turned to flight armies of aliens" uses *eklinan* (klinō), "to bend, incline" — a technical military term for routing an enemy line until it buckles and breaks.
translation: Quenched the force of fire, escaped the mouths of the sword, out of weakness were made powerful, became mighty in war, made the armies of foreigners bend and break.

label: Hebrews 11:35
text: "Were tortured" translates *etympanisthēsan* (tympanizō), a verb built directly on *tympanon*, the wheel-shaped rack over which a victim was stretched like a drumhead and then beaten. The word is brutally literal, not a generic term for suffering. These martyrs are offered a way off the rack — recant, and live — and the text marks that offer with the definite article, "the deliverance," the specific release actually on the table, which they refuse. They hold out instead for "a better resurrection," *kreittonos* (kreittōn), a comparative that measures this hope against mere restoration to ordinary life — like the widow's son raised earlier in the same verse — and finds it wanting; they wanted resurrection to glory, not simply resumed existence.
translation: Women received back their dead by resurrection; and others were racked and beaten, refusing to accept the release offered them, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

label: Hebrews 11:36
text: "Others" shifts from *allos* (used elsewhere in the chapter for "another of the same kind") to *heteroi* (heteros), "others of a different kind" — signaling a change of category, from martyrs killed outright to those who endured a slower ordeal. "Yea, moreover" translates *eti de*, a climactic formula that ratchets the list upward: after mockings and scourgings comes something the writer treats as worse still — chains and prison, the kind of confinement Jeremiah endured, a drawn-out torment of the mind rather than a single blow to the body.
translation: And still others of a different kind received trial by mockings and scourgings, and, what is more, by chains and imprisonment.

label: Hebrews 11:37
text: The rapid, unconnected rhythm continues. "They died by slaughter of the sword" points to mass killings rather than isolated executions — the kind of scenes the letter's first Jewish readers would already know well from the Maccabean persecutions. The sheepskins and goatskins were not a prophet's professional uniform; they are mentioned because these fugitives had nothing else to wear. "Afflicted" translates *thlibomenoi* (thlibō), "to press hard upon, to squeeze" — the image is of being crushed from outside; "tormented" is *kakouchoumenoi* (kakoucheō), "to treat badly, maltreat," a catch-all word for abuse covering whatever specific cruelty is not already named.
translation: They were stoned, they were tempted, they were sawn in two, they died by slaughter of the sword; they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being in want, pressed hard, treated with every kind of abuse.

label: Hebrews 11:38
text:
"World" here is *kosmos*, but not the corrupt system the word usually names elsewhere in the New Testament — it is the world considered as an ordered economy, a whole way of valuing and organizing life. That economy runs on sight and self-interest; the martyrs ran on faith, operating on an entirely different plane, so the world that drove them out into deserts and mountains turns out to be the one found wanting, not them. "Caves" translates *opais* (opē), a word that originally meant simply "a hole" or an opening one can see through — the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cleft in the rock where God hid Moses to let His glory pass by. These heroes of faith ended their lives in the same kind of hole God once used as a shelter for His own glory.

The passage insists in the same breath that this whole company "received not the promise." The verb is a plain aorist of *lambanō*, "to take, receive" — they died without the object of the promise in hand, holding only the certainty that it was coming. That gap between promise given and promise fulfilled is not a mark of failure; it is structural to the whole chapter. Every hero named here saw the goal from a distance and died still reaching toward it.

The reason supplied is striking: God had "provided some better thing for us," so that the Old Testament faithful should not be made perfect apart from us. "Made perfect" translates a form of *teleioō*, a verb this letter uses repeatedly for the finishing work accomplished by Christ's better sacrifice and better covenant — not moral improvement but the reaching of a designed goal. The grammar binds Old and New Testament believers into a single, jointly-completed company: their perfecting waits on ours, so that no stage of God's redemptive plan reaches its finish line alone.

That roll call then feeds straight into the exhortation that follows, where these figures are called a "cloud of witnesses" — *nephos*, not the sharply outlined *nephelē* but a vast, formless mass filling the whole visible sky, the very image classical writers used for an overwhelming multitude of people. "Witnesses" is *martyrōn* (martys), the term for one who testifies to what he has personally seen — these figures are less spectators in a grandstand than a bank of testimony the letter's readers are urged to draw strength from as they run their own race.
translation: Men of whom the world was not worthy — wandering in deserts and mountains, and in caves and holes of the earth. And these all, though they were borne witness to through their faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided some better thing for us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

label: Hebrews 12:2
text: The roll call of Old Testament faith in chapter 11 was building to this: past every witness in that great cloud, the writer points his readers to one supreme example. "Looking" translates *aphorao* (aphoraō), a verb built on "away from" fused to "see" — it pictures a runner wrenching his eyes off the grandstand and welding them onto the finish line, sight and mind together locked on a single point. Let that focus drift toward the crowd, and the pace slackens; the Christian life runs the same way. "Author" renders *archēgos* (archēgos), built from "to lead" and "first": not merely the originator of faith but the trailblazer, the one who runs the course first and so becomes the pattern every runner after him follows. "Finisher" is *teleioō* (teleioō), "to carry through to completion" — Jesus did not simply possess faith, He lived it out to its fullest possible expression, so that His life stands as the finished, perfect specimen of what faith looks like from start to end. The preposition behind "for the joy set before him" is *anti* (anti), whose ordinary first-century meaning is "instead of," not "in order to obtain." The joy was already His — the glory shared with the Father before the world began — and the cross was what He accepted in exchange for it, not a prize He was chasing. "Set" is *prokeimenēs* (prokeimenēs), "lying before," a joy already present and possessed, surrendered rather than pursued. And "is set down" is a perfect tense: He sat down once, His work finished, and He remains seated — no repeat performance, no further offering required. Having set Jesus before them like this, the writer immediately urges his readers to "consider" him — *analogizomai* (analogizomai), "to reckon up, weigh side by side" — the opposition he endured, called *antilogia* (antilogia), "speaking against," so that these persecuted believers might measure their own suffering against his and refuse to grow faint of heart.
translation: Looking off and away, our eyes fixed on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of the faith, who instead of the joy then lying before him endured a cross, despising its shame, and has sat down and remains seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

label: Hebrews 12:4
text: The readers had suffered under persecution, but not yet to the point of bloodshed, unlike Messiah, whose obedience carried him all the way to a bloody death on a cross. "Resist" is *antikathistēmi* (antikathistēmi), a compound meaning literally "to stand against" — a posture of opposition. "Striving" is *antagōnizomai* (antagōnizomai), "to fight agonizingly against," the word behind our "agonize": not a light skirmish but a brutal, exhausting match against the pull toward apostasy. The Proverbs quotation that follows supplies the key term for the rest of the passage — "chastening," *paideia* (paideia). This is not primarily a word for punishment; it names the whole process of raising and training a child, correcting faults and cultivating virtue toward maturity. Reading their persecution through this word reframes it entirely: not retribution for wrongdoing, but the discipline that shapes a son into what he is meant to become.
translation: Not yet have you resisted to the point of shedding blood, in your struggle against sin.

label: Hebrews 12:7
text: The word rendered "endure" is *hupomenō* (hupomenō), literally "to remain under" — the readers are pictured staying put beneath a weight rather than shrugging it off. The grammar here describes an ongoing fact, not a conditional: it is for training, not despite it, that they are remaining under these pressures. "Dealeth" translates *prospherō* (prospherō) in its passive form, "to be treated, to be behaved toward" — the very fact of God's afflictive dealing with them is itself the proof that they belong to him. This letter went out to a mixed congregation, saved and unsaved alike sitting under the same persecution. What separated the two was precisely this: who would keep remaining under the discipline, and who would bolt back to the old sacrifices to escape it.
translation: It is for training that you are remaining under it; God is dealing with you as with sons. For what son is there whom a father does not discipline?

label: Hebrews 12:8
text: Old Testament Israel had learned to read any national hardship — drought, famine, invasion — as a sign of God's displeasure. It would have been natural for these first-century Hebrews to read their persecution the same way. The writer flips the logic: far from proving God's disfavor, the discipline proves the opposite. Every genuine son gets disciplined; a household that leaves a child untouched by correction has not treated him as a son at all. Absence of discipline, not its presence, is the danger sign here.
translation: But if you are without the discipline in which all sons have shared, then you are illegitimate, and not sons.

label: Hebrews 12:9
text: The connective "furthermore" signals a shift in the argument: up to this point the comparison has run between God's fatherhood and human fatherhood generally; now the writer narrows it to make the human side look small. Our earthly fathers disciplined us according to "the flesh" — their claim on us is limited, physical, temporary — while God is called "Father of spirits," the one who generates and sustains our essential, eternal being. Human fathers we respected out of natural affection or plain fear; how much more, then, does the Father of spirits deserve our full submission? "Live" is not pushed off into some future reward — it names real, present vitality now, the difference between merely existing and actually having life.
translation: Furthermore, we have had fathers of our flesh as those who disciplined us, and we kept paying them reverence. Shall we not much more be subjecting ourselves to the Father of spirits, and live?

label: Hebrews 12:10
text: Two things mark human discipline as imperfect. First, it is confined to childhood — it stops at manhood whether or not it finished its work. Second, human parents are short-sighted and fallible; the word behind "pleasure" is *dokeō* (dokeō), "to be of the opinion, to suppose" — it names subjective judgment, guesswork that may or may not land on what is actually best. What seemed good to a parent was not always what was good for the child. God's discipline carries no such limitation. It is not guesswork but purpose, aimed at one clear end: that we come to share, in actual experience, in his own holiness.
translation: For they, on the one hand, disciplined us for a few days according to what seemed good to them; but he disciplines us for our profit, so that we may share in his holiness.

label: Hebrews 12:11
text: The negation in this verse falls on "seems," not on "chastening" — no discipline, of any kind, seems pleasant while it is happening. "Yieldeth" is *apodidōmi* (apodidōmi), "to give back" — carrying a hint of repayment, as though the harvest is compensation for what the discipline cost. "Exercised" is *gumnazō* (gumnazō), the verb behind "gymnasium," used of athletes training their bodies through repeated strain. The picture is of spiritual muscle built the same way physical muscle is built — through resistance, not comfort. What these readers were going through was, in that sense, training: the internal struggle between retreating to the old system for relief and pressing on in a faith not yet fully proven to them.
translation: Now all discipline, for the present, does not seem to be joyful but painful; yet afterward it keeps on yielding back the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

label: Hebrews 12:12
text: "Lift up" translates *anorthoō* (anorthoō), a term used by medical writers for setting a dislocated joint back into place and restoring it to strength — far more forceful than a simple "raise." These are not tired hands that need encouragement; they are joints that need to be reset. "Hang down" is *pariēmi* (pariēmi), originally "to let pass, to disregard," and by extension "to go slack" — describing hands that have simply stopped functioning, most likely in prayer, through neglect. "Feeble" is *paraluō* (paraluō), the very word behind "paralytic," the same term used of the palsied man in Matthew 8. These are not merely weary limbs; they are limbs gone numb and unresponsive, in need of active reinvigoration, not gentle encouragement.
translation: Therefore, set straight again the hands that have gone slack and the knees that have become paralyzed.

label: Hebrews 12:13
text: "Paths" is *trochia* (trochia), literally "wheel-track" — the rut a cart wears into a road. "Straight" here is *orthos* (orthos), used not in the sense of straight-versus-crooked but of level, smooth, passable — clear the ruts so nothing catches a wheel. "Lame" is *cholos* (cholos), used elsewhere of physical limping but applied here to a spiritual stagger, describing those among the readers most shaken by persecution and closest to turning back. "Turned out of the way" translates *ektrepō* (ektrepō), another term drawn from medicine, meaning "to wrench or twist out of joint" — the image is of a limping limb further injured by rough ground rather than helped over it. The exhortation is aimed at the already-faithful: live steadily enough that your example smooths the road rather than laming further those still finding their footing.
translation: And keep making straight wheel-tracks for your feet, so that what is lame may not be wrenched out of joint, but rather be healed.

label: Hebrews 12:14
text: "Follow" is *diōkō* (diōkō), "to run swiftly in pursuit, to press hard after" — the same verb Paul uses of straining toward the finish line in Philippians 3:12. There is nothing passive in it; it describes a racer's urgency applied to the pursuit of peace and holiness. Given the historical setting, the exhortation carries real bite: persecution breeds exactly the kind of resentment and division that make peace hard to chase, especially toward believers who look weak or wavering. The holiness in view is not abstract piety but the specific standing this letter has already described — a cleansed conscience, real access to God through Christ's sacrifice. Without it, no one sees the Lord.
translation: Keep constantly pursuing peace with everyone, and the holiness apart from which no one will see the Lord.

label: Hebrews 12:15
text:
"Looking diligently" translates *episkopeō* (episkopeō), the verb behind our word "bishop" and the same root used of elders exercising oversight in 1 Peter 5:2 and Acts 20:28. The prefix turns a simple "look" into "watch over, keep guard" — the readers are told to police their own condition the way an overseer watches a congregation. "Fail" is *hustereō* (hustereō) combined with "away from," giving "to fall back from" something already attained — and it is a present-tense participle, describing a drift already underway rather than a hypothetical danger. This pictures precisely the unsaved Jew who has been carried along by the Spirit's convicting work up to the very edge of faith, and who now risks slipping back rather than crossing over. "Root of bitterness" also carries a present participle — "springing up" — a process caught mid-motion, still revealing what kind of root it is as it grows, with the power to poison not just one person but, as the definite article specifies, "the many": the majority of the congregation.

The same watchfulness applies to the danger of scandal. "Profane," describing Esau, is *bebēlos* (bebēlos), a word originally used of ground open to any foot to walk on — common, unconsecrated — standing opposite *hagios* (hagios), "set apart, holy." Esau was profane not primarily in the moral sense but in this deeper sense: nothing in him was reserved for God. His birthright carried the family priesthood, and he traded it for a single meal, treating what should have been sacred as ordinary currency. The parallel to these readers is exact and uncomfortable: like Esau, they only professed to hold something — salvation — that had not yet, in the case of the unconverted among them, actually been secured, and they stood in danger of trading that profession for relief from persecution just as cheaply as Esau traded his birthright for soup.

When Esau later wanted the blessing back, Scripture records that he "found no place of repentance." Greek supplies two distinct words for repentance, and the choice here matters. *Metamelomai* (metamelomai) means regret or remorse over the consequences of an act — it is the word used of Judas. *Metanoeō* (metanoeō) means an actual reversal of moral purpose, a genuine change of mind and direction. Esau could work himself into tears of remorse; he could never work himself into that deeper reversal. The warning to the readers follows the same line as the sin of chapter 6: a hardness that forecloses on its own future, not because God's mercy runs out, but because the heart that produced it no longer wants what mercy offers.

The passage that follows sets this warning against the backdrop of Sinai itself. "Might be touched" is *psēlaphaō* (psēlaphaō), a present participle describing groping or feeling after something rather than confirmed contact — the mountain was material and reachable, but only just, and only through fear. "Blackness" and "darkness" render two different Greek words for gloom, the kind of half-dark that swallows color without erasing it entirely — dusk, or the shadow of death. "Tempest" is *thuella* (thuella), from a root meaning "to boil or foam" — a sudden, violent, upward-tearing gale, not a gentle wind. This is the old covenant's own self-portrait: a mountain wrapped in fear. The readers are being told plainly what they are not returning to.
translation: Keep exercising oversight over yourselves, so that no one may be falling back from the grace of God; so that no root of bitterness, springing up, may trouble you, and through it the many be defiled.

label: Hebrews 12:19
text: The writer keeps piling up the sensory details of Sinai — trumpet blast, an audible voice speaking actual words — to press home just how overwhelming and material that revelation was. The people who heard it did not ask for more; they begged that not one further word be added. That reaction alone tells the story: this was a revelation the hearers could not endure directly, in sharp contrast to what the readers are being invited into instead.
translation: And to a blast of a trumpet, and to a sound of words being spoken — a sound of such a kind that those who heard it begged that no further word be added to them.

label: Hebrews 12:20
text: "Touch" here is *thinganō* (thinganō), "to touch, to handle" in a way that affects the object touched — in classical usage it often describes laying hands on something sacred, an act capable of desecrating it. To touch Sinai at all, even accidentally, was to profane it, and the penalty was severe enough that it applied even to a wandering animal. The command reveals just how absolute the boundary around the old covenant's holy ground was — untouchable, on pain of death, even for a beast that could not know better.
translation: For they could not bear what was commanded: "If even a beast touches the mountain, it is to be stoned."

label: Hebrews 12:21
text: "Fear" here is intensified by its prefix — *ekphobos* (ekphobos), built on the preposition "out of" attached to "fear," meaning something closer to "frightened right out of oneself." Even Moses, who spoke with God face to face, was reduced to this by the sight at Sinai. If the mediator of the old covenant reacted this way, the writer's point about what that revelation actually felt like from the inside needs no further argument.
translation: And so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, "I am frightened out of myself, and trembling."

label: Hebrews 12:22–24
text:
Against that terrifying backdrop, the writer swings the readers toward the opposite picture entirely: not a mountain wrapped in dread but a city alive with celebration. "General assembly" translates *panēguris* (panēguris), a classical term for a festival gathering of an entire people turned out for public games or a national celebration — the word itself carries a note of festivity that has nothing in common with Sinai's gloom. "Church" is *ekklēsia* (ekklēsia), "a called-out assembly" — here naming the whole company of the redeemed, and "the spirits of just men made perfect" names specifically those already gone ahead into glory. Every phrase in this list functions as a deliberate counterweight to the fire, blackness, and trumpet-blast just described: angels beyond counting instead of terror, festival instead of dread, access instead of a boundary line no one dared cross.

Best of all, this whole gathering centers on Jesus himself, called here "mediator of a new covenant" and connected to "the blood of sprinkling." The comparison is not between Christ's blood and the blood that literally flowed from Abel's own body — it is between Christ's blood and the animal blood Abel offered in sacrifice. The entire letter has been building toward exactly this claim: that the blood of the new covenant does not merely equal but supersedes and replaces every drop shed under the old sacrificial system. Abel's offering could only point forward; this one actually accomplishes what it points to.
translation: But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem, and to countless myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and to God, judge of all, and to the spirits of righteous ones made perfect, and to Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, and to blood that speaks something better than Abel's.

label: Hebrews 12:26
text: At Sinai, God's voice shook the physical earth — a single, historical, localized event. The promise the writer now quotes from Haggai points to something larger still on the horizon: a coming shaking that will not stop at the earth but will reach the heavens themselves. What was once a mountain trembling under a voice becomes, in this prophecy, the entire created order set trembling under the same voice — the same God who spoke through angels at Sinai now speaks through his own Son, and one day that voice will unmake and remake the whole universe.
translation: Whose voice then shook the earth; but now he has given a promise, on record, saying, "Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven."

label: Hebrews 12:27
text:
The writer zeroes in on one phrase from the Haggai quotation — "yet once more" — because of what it implies: this final shaking is final, a last event before the eternal order is established. "Removing" translates *metatithēmi* (metatithēmi), "to transfer to a new basis, to transpose" — not a word for annihilation but for exchange, moving something from one footing onto another. What gets shaken is everything that was ever made, the entire created order under the weight of the curse; what remains is whatever cannot be shaken in the first place. The point is not destruction for its own sake but clarification: stripping away the temporary reveals what was eternal all along.

On the strength of that permanence, the readers are told to hold onto grace and offer God worship marked by *eulabeia* (eulabeia) — not timidity but careful, deliberate reverence — and by *deos* (deos), a wholesome, sobered awe, deliberately distinct from *phobos* (phobos), the cringing terror of someone facing raw danger. "Consuming fire" is not decoration; it names the same holiness that once wrapped Sinai in smoke, a holiness that will not coexist indefinitely with persistent, unrepented evil. For a congregation being tempted to trade the reality of Christ's sacrifice for the shadow of the old one, the warning and the comfort arrive in the very same sentence.
translation: And this phrase, "yet once more," signals the transposing onto a new basis of the things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, so that the things not shaken may remain.

label: Hebrews 13:2
text: "Hospitality" translates *philoxenia* (philoxenia), literally "love of strangers" — *phileo* (to love, be fond of) fused with *xenos* (a stranger or foreign guest). The command "be not forgetful" uses a negated present imperative, which in Greek prohibits an ongoing lapse rather than a single slip: not "don't forget this once" but "stop letting it drop — keep it up." The reward clause trades on a verb meaning "to escape notice": some, without realizing what they were doing, ended up hosting angels as houseguests. The point rests on real uncertainty — you can't always tell, from the outside, who you're feeding.
translation: Do not keep on forgetting hospitality to strangers, for through this some, without knowing it, entertained angels as guests.

label: Hebrews 13:3
text: "Be mindful" is a present imperative — a standing habit of attention, not a passing glance. "As bound with them" comes from a perfect passive participle built on *deo* (deo, "to bind") with the prefix *syn* ("together with"): readers are told to picture themselves chained alongside the prisoner, not merely sympathizing from outside the cell. The final phrase, "in the body," grounds the whole appeal in something unavoidably physical — you too wear flesh that can be seized and starved, so the sufferer's body is to be treated as continuous with your own.
translation: Keep on being mindful of those in prison, as though bound together with them; of those being mistreated, since you yourselves also are in a body.

label: Hebrews 13:4
text:
Greek often drops the verb "to be," and this verse is a case in point — the writer supplies none, leaving translators to decide whether he states a fact or gives an order. Context favors a command: a present imperative, "let marriage be held..." "Honor" is *timios* (timios), literally "of great price" — the word for something so valuable it is prized rather than merely respected. The purity of the marriage bed follows as the natural consequence of that valuation, not as a separate rule bolted on.

The next verses pivot to money and trust. "Without covetousness" is the compound *aphilarguros* (aphilarguros) — an alpha-negative plus *phileo* ("to love") plus *arguros* ("silver"): "without any fondness for silver." "Content" translates *arkeo* (arkeo), a verb meaning to possess enough strength in oneself to lack nothing needed; its cognate noun gave the Stoics their word for self-sufficiency, but here the sufficiency is not self-generated — it rests on dependence on God rather than willpower.

The promise that follows stacks up negatives for emphasis, since Greek grammar lets multiple negatives intensify a denial rather than cancel it out — the line reads less like a flat future tense and more like "I will absolutely not, not ever." "Forsake" is built from *leipo* ("to leave") with two prefixes, *kata* ("down") and *en* ("in") — the compound pictures abandoning someone helpless in the middle of a bad situation, not simply walking away from them.
translation: Let marriage be held as precious among all, and let the marriage bed be kept undefiled; for God will judge sexually immoral persons and adulterers.

label: Hebrews 13:7
text: "Remember" is again a present imperative — an ongoing discipline of calling former leaders to mind, not a one-time memorial. "Follow" renders a verb meaning "imitate," aimed specifically at their faith, while "considering" is a compound built on *theoreo* ("to look at") with the prefix *ana* ("up, thoroughly") — a careful, sustained inspection, not a glance in passing. "The end of their conversation" is better read as the outcome of their way of life: readers are told to watch how a life anchored in that faith actually finished, and to copy the parts of it that matched what was taught.
translation: Keep remembering those leading you, who spoke to you the word of God; and, carefully observing the outcome of their way of life, keep imitating their faith.

label: Hebrews 13:8
text: No verb "is" appears in the Greek, so the natural reading pairs "Jesus" directly with "Christ" as a claim of identity: Jesus is the Messiah. "Christ" simply transliterates the Greek word for "anointed," carrying over the sense of the Hebrew "Messiah" — not a title tacked onto a name but a translated claim about who this man is. Since the leaders just mentioned had staked their lives on exactly that identification, the writer is holding up their unwavering conviction as much as he is asserting Christ's own changelessness.
translation: Jesus is the Messiah — yesterday and today the same, and forever.

label: Hebrews 13:9
text: "Be not carried about" is a negated present passive imperative — a command to stop something already in progress: readers were actively being swept along by these teachings as the letter reached them. "Divers and strange" pairs a word for "many-colored, variegated" with a word for "foreign" — the danger isn't one clean, identifiable error but a shifting patchwork of them, none of it native to the gospel. The heart is "established" by a verb built on the idea of firmness — grace makes it steady in a way food regulations never could, since those who relied on the latter got no lasting benefit from it.
translation: Stop being carried away by teachings that are many-colored and foreign to the faith. For it is good for the heart to keep being made steady by grace, not by foods, which never profited those devoted to them.

label: Hebrews 13:10
text: "Right" translates *exousia* (exousia), a legal term for delegated authority — the standing to do something because it has been granted, not mere ability to do it. The claim is pointed: those still serving at the Levitical tabernacle have no legal claim on this altar's food, because the two systems simply don't overlap. "Serve" here is the technical verb for cultic ministry, covering priest and worshiper alike — anyone still operating inside the old system is shut out of the new one's table by definition, not as a penalty.
translation: We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat.

label: Hebrews 13:11
text: The verbs describing the Day of Atonement ritual sit in the present tense, marking a fixed, repeated pattern rather than a single past event: the blood "is brought" in by the high priest, the carcasses "are burned" outside the camp. That habitual present matters for the argument — this was never a one-off but the standing rule of the old system, and the rule itself excluded any sacrificial meal for priest or people alike.
translation: For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought by the high priest into the sanctuary as a sin offering are burned up outside the camp.

label: Hebrews 13:12
text:
"Sanctify" is *hagiazo* (hagiazo), "to set apart for God," and here it stands as an aorist subjunctive inside a purpose clause — a single, decisive act aimed at a specific goal, not a gradual process. "His own blood" uses the possessive *idios* (idios), stressing that the blood was peculiarly his, personally his own, not merely available to him. "Suffered" is likewise aorist, a completed historical event: Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem's gate, matching the disposal of the Day of Atonement carcasses outside the camp, so that his death would set apart a people cut loose from the old system's boundaries.

The verses that follow press the application: believers are to keep going out to him outside the camp, carrying his reproach, because "here" — on earth, inside the old order — there is no city that remains. The earthly city is described with a present participle meaning "the one presently remaining," set against a future participle meaning "the one about to come." The old order is temporary by grammar as well as by fact.
translation: Therefore Jesus also, in order that he might set apart the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.

label: Hebrews 13:17
text:
The verse issues two present imperatives, "obey" and "submit" — a habitual posture, not a single act of compliance. "Submit" is itself a compound meaning literally "to retreat under," picturing a voluntary yielding of ground rather than a forced defeat. The leaders "watch" using a verb built from "without sleep" — the image is of someone keeping vigil through the night, the way a shepherd or a nurse stays alert over a case that cannot be left unattended. Their eventual accounting is described with *apodidomi* (apodidomi), a verb at home in commerce and bookkeeping, "to pay back what is owed" — cast here as a future participle: they are people who will one day have to render this account, and that expectation shapes how closely they watch now.

The writer wants that watch kept "with joy, not with groaning" — the groan he names is the particular sigh of someone shouldering a thankless, resisted task. And the closing clause turns on a rare compound, *alysiteles* (alysiteles), built on the negative of a word meaning "profitable" or "paying its toll" — resisting these leaders, the writer says, is a losing transaction, unprofitable to the very people doing the resisting.
translation: Keep obeying your leaders and keep submitting to them, for they keep watch, sleepless, over your souls, as those who will have to render an account — so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be no profit to you.

label: Hebrews 13:22
text: "Suffer" here means "bear with" — the verb is *anechomai* (anechomai), literally "to hold oneself up under" something. The writer is asking for patient endurance of his exhortation, not mere passive tolerance. "I have written" is *epistello* (epistello), the verb for sending formal instructions by letter, and it's the root behind the word "epistle" — it names the whole document as a dispatched message, not casual correspondence. Calling the letter "few words" is itself a small apology, asking readers not to hold its brevity against the weight of what it says.
translation: And I urge you, brothers, bear with this word of exhortation, for indeed I have written to you in few words.

label: Hebrews 13:23
text: There's little grammar to mine in these closing lines, but one detail stands out: "set at liberty" is a perfect passive participle of *apolyo* (apolyo, "to release") — the perfect tense marks a completed action whose result still holds, so the writer isn't only reporting that Timothy was once freed but that he remains free as this is written. Beyond that, this is plain personal news — travel plans and a hoped-for reunion, nothing coded in the tenses.
translation: Know that our brother Timothy has been set free and remains so; if he comes soon, I will see you along with him.
